*5th place (gold) in [Kaggriculture](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture), team 有辣条有权.*

| Looking for | Go to |
|---|---|
| What we did, technique by technique, with links to the code | [HOW-IT-WORKS.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/HOW-IT-WORKS.md) |
| Every feature, and the solvers that compute them | [FEATURES.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/FEATURES.md) |
| The code that matters, flat and grouped: features, Model 1, Model 2 | [code/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/code) (Model 1 [`model.py`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/code/model1/model.py), Model 2 [`nf_model.py`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/code/model2/nf_model.py)) |
| Training on one replay, end to end | [quickstart/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/quickstart) |
| How games were collected, filtered and sampled | [data/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/data) |
| The submitted agents, and how candidates were compared | [submissions/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/submissions) · [evaluation/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/evaluation) |
| Rebuilding both submissions from scratch | [REPRODUCE.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/REPRODUCE.md) |

## Intro

This covers my attempt at using SFT to solve Kaggriculture. It assumes the vocabulary in the [competition overview](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/overview).

I don't quote leaderboard scores. The Elo-style rating only means something relative to the field at the time: a bot of the same strength would score several hundred points lower later on, because the field as a whole got stronger as time went on, and the rate of improvement increased closer to the deadline, especially once a lot of people moved to using all four quadrants in the last three days.

I mostly document what worked. Plenty didn't, and I don't keep meticulous logs of what failed. Each failure still cost real time. For example, I spent two weeks factoring the game's micro decisions into macro decisions, down to a page of theorems on how to handle them (311 claims, 919 linked pairs). This is the approach I really wanted to take, but it proved too much for agents to keep track of at once, even after I simplified it for them. They still made very subtle mistakes. I imagine this method will work once agents get stronger.

## Resources

I enter each competition to win or learn as much as possible, within a budget. Here: two 4090s I own, a 3090 (that kept dying), a DGX Spark and a laptop 4060 for eval games, Colab G4s rented on 29 and 30 Sep, and Kaggle CPU notebooks for evals. I have two Claude and two GPT subscriptions. These resources are shared among all my projects, including personal ones.

If I had more compute, I would have used it.

Team name: **有辣条有权** ("you la tiao you quan"). La tiao is a famous cheap spicy snack, and the name is a play on **有钱有权** ("you qian you quan"): "To have money is to have power." Swap 钱 (qian, money) for 辣条 (la tiao) and you get the team name.

## Models

These were my two final submissions. The larger, longer-trained B-even model finished ahead of N-flow and set the team's placing.

### Abandoned

The macro approach went first, so I won't discuss the architectures I considered there. Everything below came after I switched to micro decisions generated autoregressively. I had [this lecture series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SQ3fZ1sAqXI&list=PLoROMvodv4rOY23Y0BoGoBGgQ1zmU_MT_) playing in the background, and it drove the switch. This game doesn't seem that different from writing a paragraph in a very specific style.

I train on the state the winner saw and the actions they sent. During play, the model generates worker commands, then orders, then STOP, one token at a time, with each token seeing the earlier choices from that turn.

Other failures:

1. **Chain of thought:** force an unsupervised label onto every tile before deciding.
2. **Recurrence in depth:** rerun the middle blocks several times. Showed a lot of promise early, with some of our best losses, but needed too many ablations to get right. No time to tune how many times, or which layers, to recur, and it ended up doing poorly late with the config I chose. Something I'll try earlier next time.
3. **Depth over width:** worse loss immediately.
4. **Massive parallel heads:** 36 heads of width 12. Did very well and only started to do poorly later, which leads to Model 1.

### Model 1: B-even

The 36-head model with its heads regrouped to 18 × 24. Shipped with a 4-update sprinkle on the five newest #1-team wins.

### Model 2: N flow

Random init on one G4. Shipped with a 15-min wash: low-learning-rate SFT on top-3 wins.

## Features

## Data

How the SFT data was filtered and changed:

- **Winners only.** Never imitate a losing action. In games we lost, train on the player who beat us.
- **Weighted to fresh and strong.** Hourly buckets by day and rank; the newest and strongest games get most of the draws.
- **Earlier, our own ladder games too.** Whatever beat our policy became training data.
- **Last day: top 3 only.** 30 Sep wins by the top three teams (404 source seats); the seats that beat #1 count 4x.
- **Short top-ups.** 15 minutes at low LR on the newest winners, exporting the current, unaveraged weights (RAW).
- **Held out.** Validation and sealed games were excluded early. Some validation games entered the late pool.

We could only find 3 wins against the first-place solution at the time we trained, and two of them were from its own validation games!

Replays came from Kaggle's daily episode dumps. The replay API was only for our own losses, and on the last two days for everything, at ~150-170 an hour. I also tried pulling replays by hand on the website: similar rate, but the API was less boring :D

## Biggest lesson

What I think was most useful was the workflow I refined during this competition, and will keep refining going forward.

Keep 2-3 ideas alive. Each has a fallback, a current best and a current experiment. Go crazy with the experiment until it beats the best, then try a new crazy experiment. Once you've experimented enough, the best becomes the new fallback. An experiment can itself be a set of ideas, so it's basically tree search over ideas.

Finally, we used a special version of the engine for matched games, so that shop rolls depend only on the initial seed.

## Code

Everything needed to rebuild both final submissions from the Kaggle episodes is in this repo. The episodes themselves are not included; they come from Kaggle. See [REPRODUCE.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/REPRODUCE.md). To jump from an idea in this write-up to the code that implements it, use [HOW-IT-WORKS.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/HOW-IT-WORKS.md).

| Folder | What |

| [`code/`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/code) | start here to read: byte-identical copies of the ~50 files that matter, flat and grouped |
| [`quickstart/`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/quickstart) | start here to run: one replay → features → a few training updates for each model |
| [`submissions/`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/submissions) | the two final archives exactly as submitted, plus their unpacked inference code |
| [`data/`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/data) | episode download, replay processing, winner-seat selection, buckets and rosters |
| [`model1-b-even/`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/model1-b-even) | Model 1 training code and every stage from random init to the shipped checkpoint |

---

I fine-tuned a LoRA on 1,500 trajectories from the reference agent. On Kaggle it scored 0.0: the model spent four minutes before its first tool call, then repeated the same `git log` command until the budget ran out, and submitted nothing. The cause was the LoRA scaling factor, not the data. The full path, including the part where I benchmarked the wrong model for four hours, is below.

## Why this exists

The competition gives you a 31B Gemma 4 checkpoint, a set of repositories with hidden tests, and a harness that runs an agent against them. LoRA adapters are allowed, which makes the obvious move tempting: take a stronger agent, record what it does, and teach the smaller one to imitate it.

So I did that. This post is the result, including the part where the fine-tune turned out to be worse than the model it was supposed to improve.

If you are planning a LoRA for this competition, the short version is: check your adapter scaling before you check anything else.

## Data

I started from the public tasks that ship with the competition, plus a set of extra tasks from the same repositories that I extracted separately and attached to the local harness. Each task comes with a repository snapshot pinned at the base commit, so a run is reproducible.

For every task I ran the reference agent from the sample submission at five sampling temperatures between 0.2 and 1.0. That produced roughly 1,500 transcripts. Most of them are not usable, and the filtering mattered more than the generation:

- I kept only runs the harness scored as resolved.
- For each task I kept a single trajectory, the shortest by tool-call count. This keeps the context under 32k and, more importantly, avoids teaching the model to wander.
- I dropped repositories where the harness itself misbehaved (networkx snapshots, urllib3, cmd2). Training on a broken verifier teaches noise.

The result was 697 training examples from 99 tasks, plus 60 held-out examples from 11 tasks that do not appear in the training set. Same repositories, different tasks, so the held-out number is optimistic about unseen repositories but honest about unseen issues.

Every example is a message list plus the nine tool schemas. The system prompt is the exact 3,728-character prompt used at inference, not a rewritten one. And there are no thinking traces anywhere in the data: the reference agent's transcripts contain tool calls and short commentary, nothing else. That detail comes back later and bites.

## Training

One practical problem first: PEFT cannot attach to the packaged `gemma-4-31b-it-qat-w4a16-ct` checkpoint. I trained on a dequantized bf16 copy of it instead, which is the closest thing to the scored model that accepts an adapter.

The model I fine-tuned is the full bf16 checkpoint, not a quantized one. The 4-bit setting below only describes how the frozen base was loaded into memory during training. Nothing inside the adapter is quantized.

The recipe:

- the frozen base loaded in 4-bit nf4 with nested quantization (QLoRA)
- the adapter itself is plain bf16: 245 MB, 820 tensors
- rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05
- all seven projections: q, k, v, o, gate, up, down, across all 60 layers
- 410 adapted modules, 122.4M trainable parameters
- FFPA attention kernel, enabled through a small `sitecustomize` shim and `attn_implementation: "ffpa"`
- 3 epochs, learning rate 1e-4 with cosine decay and 20 warmup steps
- batch size 1, gradient accumulation 4, bf16, Liger kernel, packing disabled
- `max_length: 32768`, because a truncated trajectory teaches the model to stop mid-sentence

The hardware was two ASUS GX10 boxes with one GPU each, training across both machines. The planned run was 264 optimizer steps; I stopped at 220 to free the GPUs, so the final learning-rate anneal never finished.

One detail worth spelling out, because it trips people up. TRL's `assistant_only_loss` needs `{% generation %}` markers around the assistant tokens in the chat template, and the stock Gemma 4 template has none. I made a copy of the template and inserted the markers. The token stream itself does not change; only the label mask does. I verified this later by rendering the same conversation with the stock template and with the patched one: 12,602 tokens in both cases, zero divergence. So the template is not a hidden variable here.

The loss curve on the held-out split: 0.6126, 0.5483, 0.5201, 0.5088. Monotone improvement, no sign of overfitting. This is the last number in this post that looks good.

## The adapter in the wild

I deployed with vLLM. On Kaggle that is 4×L4 with vLLM 0.19.1 and the official `-ct` weights. Locally it is two GX10 machines with tensor parallelism 2, MTP speculative decoding and a 32k context, serving the same QAT checkpoint. In both cases the adapter sits on top as a separate bf16 LoRA.

The first submission scored zero. The log told a strange story. The model spent 257 seconds before its first tool call, then started issuing the same command over and over, swapping one keyword at a time:

```
git log --all --oneline | grep -i "release_prep"
git log --all --oneline | grep -i "release_ready"
git log --all --oneline | grep -i "release_now"
```

It burned the entire 24-call budget that way, then emitted a long stream of empty tool calls that the harness rejected with `error (exit 0)`, and submitted nothing. It never made a single edit.

I assumed the harness was at fault. There are two well-known problems in this setup that look plausible: a tool-argument parser that can loop on malformed array arguments, and a context-overflow path that skips the fallback `git diff` capture. Neither applied. The commands were well-formed and the context never overflowed.

## Isolating the cause

The same task, same budgets, same snapshots, run without the adapter: normal behaviour, patch in 15 calls, tests pass. With the adapter: the loop.

Then I went down the list. Chat template: identical rendering, ruled out. Tool schemas: identical to training, ruled out. NaN or infinity in the weights: none. Adapter shape: 410 modules across all 60 layers, exactly as trained. Parser: the array-argument case never fired.

What actually fixed it was the LoRA scaling factor.

## Alpha is a real knob, and it is not obvious

LoRA adds one term to each adapted layer:

```
h = W·x + (alpha / r) · B(A(x))
```

With rank 16 and alpha 32, the scale is 2.0. The adapter's correction is applied at double strength. That is legal, and it is what the training objective was optimized for, but it is also enough to push the model out of distribution.

**Alpha 32, scale 2.0.** Degenerate. Repetition loops, four minutes before the first tool call, empty patches, score zero. Not a subtle degradation either: the model stops behaving like an agent and starts behaving like an n-gram model with a budget.

**Alpha 16, scale 1.0.** The loops disappear entirely. This is the configuration I would call "the model the training intended": the full learnable correction at its nominal strength. The side effect is that it gets slower and more deliberate. Thinking blocks grow from a couple of hundred characters to 2,500–14,700 characters per step, and median time per task went from 163 seconds at alpha 8 to 290 seconds at alpha 16. It solved one task the base model could not, textual-3659, with a clean 1,727-character patch and 61 passing tests. But it also started timing out on tasks it used to finish, because thinking eats the wall clock.

**Alpha 8, scale 0.5.** The safest setting. No loops, fastest of the three (median 163 seconds), and it produces a patch on every single task, even the ones it fails. But it only applies a quarter of the learned correction, so it is really an interpolation halfway between the base model and the fine-tune. It solves a few tasks the base misses and loses a few the base solves.

The important thing is that alpha is not baked into the weights. It is applied at inference, it is one line in `adapter_config.json`, and it requires only a server restart. If your fine-tune behaves like a broken model, sweep alpha from 8 to 32 before you conclude anything about your data. I lost a week because I did not.

## Numbers

These are all on tasks from the training set, so treat them as a sanity check, not as a leaderboard estimate.

| Configuration | Solved | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Base model, no adapter | 8 / 11 | Reference point |
| LoRA, alpha 32 | 0 / 1 | Repetition loop, no patch |
| LoRA, alpha 8 | 6 / 11 | Always patches, sometimes faster, loses some base wins |
| LoRA, alpha 16, 24 calls / 6 min | 5 / 8 | Loops gone, noticeably more thinking |
| LoRA, alpha 16, 32 calls / 8 min | 7 / 11 | One win the base misses, three losses that are budget artifacts |

Average time per task across all local runs was around 200 seconds, roughly 3.4 minutes at the looser budget. Extrapolated to 129 tasks, that is 7 to 9 hours depending on the machine, which fits the 12-hour GPU limit but without much margin.

## Two findings that generalize

**The budget is part of the prompt.** The system prompt contains a block that states the allowance explicitly:

```
## Task Budget (Session terminates when any budget is exhausted)
- Tool calls allowance: 24 calls
- Time allowance: 6.0 minutes
```

And further down it says, more importantly:

```
Plan by phases, not fixed numbers: locate & read ≈ first third;
first SOURCE edit by ≈ the middle; verify, fix, git diff,
submit_patch in the last third.
```

The plan is proportional to the allowance. That means raising the cap from 24 to 32 does not give the model more room to finish; it gives it more room to explore, in proportion. I watched this happen twice on the same task: at 24 calls it tried to edit on call 24 and was refused, at 32 calls it tried on call 32 and was refused. The bug was found both times. The fix never landed.

If you want the model to edit earlier, the cap is the wrong lever. Either the training data needs shorter exploration phases, or the prompt needs a hard instruction with a fixed number in it, which then diverges from the data the adapter was trained on.

**My training data had no thinking, but inference had it on.** Every training example ends the assistant turn with text and tool calls. There are zero thought tokens in 697 examples. At inference I was running with a thinking budget of 4,096. That is a mismatch I introduced myself, and at alpha 16 it shows up as enormous thought blocks and timeouts. If I retrain, I either generate the trajectories with thinking enabled or turn thinking off at inference. I would not mix.

**And one artifact worth naming:** `error (exit 0)` in the harness log is not a tool failure. It is what the harness prints for tool calls made after the budget is exhausted. Every task where I saw a wall of empty tool calls had already spent its allowance.

## What I would do differently

- Sweep alpha before writing a single line of new training code. It is a ten-minute experiment and it can invalidate an entire week of conclusions.
- Verify the adapter is actually attached. My first local benchmark silently ran the base model for four hours, because `agent.yaml` did not reference the adapter. The submission directory had the weights; the resolver never saw them. Check the traces for the adapter name, not just the server logs: vLLM labels every request with the base model name, so `/metrics` will not tell you.
- Evaluate on held-out tasks from day one. Training-set numbers are reassuring and meaningless.
- Filter trajectories by more than length. The reference agent spends roughly two thirds of its calls exploring, and the adapter learned that habit faithfully. On a 24-call budget, two thirds of the budget is not enough to finish.
- Do not trust the eval loss. 0.5088 is a beautiful number, and it produced a model that repeats itself until the budget runs out.

## Closing

The honest summary: in my setup the LoRA did not beat the base model. It is faster when it works, it always produces something, and it occasionally solves a task the base misses, but the aggregate is a wash. The useful output of this work is not the adapter, it is the diagnosis path: scoring factor first, template second, budget third, and only then the data.

I will be straight with you: I am a bit tired of this project, and I have a day job, so I am not going to keep grinding on it. If someone wants to take it further — retrain with thinking traces in the data, cut the exploration phase out of the trajectories, sweep alpha and rank properly, or throw the whole adapter away and just prompt the base model harder — you are welcome to it. The notebook reproduces every number in this post, including the runs that failed, so you can start from what I have instead of from zero.

If you do find something that beats the base model, I would genuinely like to read about it.

The advantage of TFMs (tabular foundation models) is that we do not need to feature engineer nor train them. We just immediately predict test data using them without having to do anything! Current TFMs perform very well as is, discussion [here][1].

# Finetuning
TFMs are NN, so we can finetune the TFM and update their model weights using train data. Some TFM libraries already have finetuning functionality. For the ones that do not, we can ask Claude Code Opus5.5 to write code for us. We observe that every TFM improves with finetuning:

| Model | Zero-shot OOF | **Fine-tuned OOF** | Δ (×1e-4) | GPU h (fine-tune + infer) | Recipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| TabPFN-3.5 | 0.961145 | **0.961248** | +1.0 | 9.8 (5.5 + 4.3) | official FinetunedTabPFNClassifier; 100k-row chunks; early stop on full-context inner val |
| Kumo-Tabular large | 0.960036 | **0.960378** | +3.4 | 9.6 (5.5 + 4.1) | own loop (Kumo train-mode forward); **lr 3e-6** (lr 1e-5 peaked at epoch 1-2 then fell: 5-fold 0.960027); 30k chunks, layer checkpointing; full-context inner val, patience 3 |
| **XGBoost (tuned)** | — | **0.959852** | — | 0.82 | GBDT, 8-seed average |
| **RealMLP (tuned)** | — | **0.959311** | — | 4.48 | MLP, 8-seed average (each seed = 8 networks, n_ens 8) |
| LimiX-2 | 0.958474 | **0.959150** | +6.8 | 31.3 (8.5 + 22.8) | own loop (prepare_cls, 2 of the 8 light pipelines per step); 50k chunks, checkpointing; 100k-context inner val |
| TabFM 1.0 | 0.958871 | **0.959109** | +2.4 | 18.2 (10.7 + 7.5) | own loop (fp32 master, bf16 autocast); 40k chunks, 1 member/step, checkpointing; 200k-context inner val |

| Kumo-Tabular small | 0.958484 | **0.958783** | +3.0 | 2.5 (1.5 + 1.0) | own loop (Kumo train-mode forward); 40k chunks, checkpointing; full-context inner val |
| Causilo | 0.958275 | **0.958713** | +4.4 | 2.8 (1.8 + 0.9) | own loop (ModelRunner with grad); 60k chunks, checkpointing; full-context inner val |
| Mitra-v2 | 0.957075 | **0.958373** | +13.0 | 37.3 (17.2 + 20.2) | own loop per AutoGluon member (8 members); 10k chunks, 10 epochs; 100k-context inner val |
| TabICLv2 | 0.958088 | **0.958351** | +2.6 | 5.5 (4.3 + 1.2) | official FinetunedTabICLClassifier; 30k chunks (CUDA grid limit ~32k x 2 estimators) |

# Configuration
Common settings: AdamW lr 1e-5 (Kumo large 3e-6; wd 0.01), cosine schedule with 10% warmup, grad clip 1; each step = one chunk of training rows (80% context, 20% query; loss on the query rows); every training row is used once per epoch. **The chunk size is the main lever**: small chunks (6k-10k) often hurt or did nothing at full context; 24k-100k chunks (with activation checkpointing where needed) gave the gains above. 

After finetuning, each TFM is then inferred with `n_estimators=8`, `full context`, and `mixed precision`.

# 70th place: Replay BC, teacher selection, and a tomato rule

Our team, **NSK_54**, finished **70th out of 10,148 teams**. This write-up focuses on the replay-BC agent that set our final score: **4883.6 private**, with a public rating of **2612.0**. The private and public ratings use different scales.

Our final agent combined a **6.54M-parameter recurrent entity Transformer**, behavior cloning from public replays, and a small deterministic overlay. The biggest improvements came from choosing **strong, current teachers with compatible strategies**.

## The final agent

We represented the observation as **277 entity tokens**: one global token, 12 item tokens, 200 farm tiles, 32 own-unit slots, and 32 opponent-unit slots. Only public opponent information was included.

The encoder used four Transformer blocks, width 256, eight attention heads, and FFN width 1024. A pooled representation updated a **256-dimensional GRU** once per turn. Two single-block autoregressive decoders generated:

- Worker commands, in engine order: farmer first, then farmhands.
- Up to ten market orders, attending to both the board and the decoded worker commands.

Each decision was factorized into **operation → item → quantity**, where applicable.

After every choice, we updated a **shadow state** tracking stock, seeds, changed tiles, cash, hires, and market supply. The next decision received legality masks and features from that updated state. This prevented reuse of stock already consumed by another worker and allowed a sale to fund a later purchase in the same turn.

The network chose routes, work allocation, investments, and sales. The shadow handled local validity and accounting; it could not prevent every strategic mistake, such as two workers walking toward the same distant tile.

Inference was greedy. In one paired test with identical weights, greedy decoding scored **0.836**, versus **0.094** with temperature-1 sampling. Small sampled errors accumulated into failed economies.

Throughout this post, local **score = (wins + 0.5 × draws) / games**.

## Replay preparation

Our initial clean top-30 dataset contained **4,290 player trajectories**, or **3,084,510 observation–action pairs**, from 18 teams. Each trajectory contained one player's 719 decisions.

We re-simulated recorded games to reconstruct observations, aligned each observation with the following replay action entry, and converted commands into **what the engine actually executed**. Every converted trajectory had to reproduce both players' next observations when its labels were decoded and replayed.

Market positions required special care. Strong teachers often submitted standing SELL orders for goods they did not hold. Approximately 10% of elite teachers' submitted SELL orders executed nothing in one audit.

We represented those orders as positional **SKIPs**. Removing them would shift subsequent orders: the engine processes both players' market lists by index, so position affects execution timing.

We also tracked exact team identities and submission versions, filtered invalid games and incompatible engine versions, deduplicated episodes, and excluded evaluation seeds. Both seats of an episode stayed in the same data split. Ordinary teacher losses were retained.

## Choosing compatible teachers

The first observation was **identical across seeds**. A greedy policy therefore made the same opening decision in every game. When we mixed teachers with incompatible openings, the student sometimes combined purchases from one strategy with labor allocation from another.

One failed opening spent **2,893 of the initial 3,000 coins**, then lost its animals by day three. Small changes near an opening logit tie could change every rollout at once.

We grouped teacher versions into families using their **turn-0/turn-1 order signatures**. An early mixed-family fine-tune lost all 32 games against our scripted reference, while a compatible-family fine-tune won **107/128**, scoring 0.836.

Compatibility alone was insufficient. A later comparison kept the architecture, initialization, budget, and learning-rate schedule fixed while changing teacher strength within the same opening family:

| Teachers | Wins against the wheat-dump reference |
| --- | ---: |
| Current top-30, compatible family | 0/32 |
| Current top-eight, compatible family | 60/64 |

The top-eight teachers differed in investment pace, market behavior, and later execution, despite similar openings.

Our successful training chain progressively narrowed the demonstrations:

| Stage | Data | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broad pretraining | 4,290 clean top-30 trajectories | Selected checkpoint after 14 epochs |
| Compatible-family refinement | Strong and elite teacher tiers | 18k + 9k updates |
| Current top-eight refinement | 877 compatible trajectories | 6k updates |
| Final specialist fine-tune | Newest compatible DSM, DECEM, and yuto083 versions | 12k updates |

The final dataset contained **213 trajectories, 197 for training**. Those 197 trajectories were the last fine-tuning set, following broad pretraining and intermediate refinement.

Adding older compatible data diluted the result. Several highly ranked off-family teachers also damaged the policy. For our model and budget, teacher compatibility, strength, and exact version mattered more than dataset size alone.

### Training details

We used masked cross-entropy over worker and market operation/item/quantity factors, with teacher-forced prefixes. A nominal update contained **eight trajectories × 64 turns = 512 rows**. GRU state was carried between chunks and detached at their boundaries.

AdamW used weight decay 0.01. Peak pretraining learning rate was 3e-4; the final fine-tunes decayed from 3e-5 to 5e-6.

Two smaller details helped define the training recipe:

- **Repeated-history weighting:** identical history prefixes received row weight `min(1, 25/m)`, where `m` was their multiplicity. This reduced repeated-opening dominance while preserving later unique behavior.
- **Fixed loss denominators:** normalizing each chunk separately had given the short 15-turn tail chunk about 4.3 times the per-row influence of a full chunk. We switched to fixed denominators.

These changes entered alongside the teacher-tier pipeline, so we did not isolate their individual contributions.

## The wheat dump: more targeted data made things worse

Eight of one BC version's first nine Kaggle losses came against opponents selling at least 20 wheat on turn zero. We reproduced the failure with a scripted opponent that submitted a large opening wheat sale.

The sale depressed wheat prices and squeezed our opening liquidity. Our policy reached zero cash, bought small amounts of feed, and fed animals that were not yet at risk. A cow unfed since day zero died at turn 48.

Our first hypothesis was missing coverage. We devoted **30% of a fine-tuning mixture** to teacher wins against these openings. It regressed:

| Attempt | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Targeted teacher wins against dump openers | Paired score change **−0.286**, 95% CI **[−0.531, −0.040]** |
| Current top-eight compatible teachers, including newer openings | **64/64 wins** on fresh seeds, mean margin about **+20.1k coins** |

The targeted model's own bank actually rose, but its market behavior helped the opponent even more. In a shared market, higher own income is an incomplete metric.

In this experiment, extra teacher examples did not teach reliable recovery from the student's mistakes. Stronger current teachers, including a more robust opening, were more effective.

## Detours: macro executors and RL

A macro-task policy produced our first major improvement. Instead of predicting individual movement steps, it predicted a task and destination, while a persistent executor handled routing and reservations. Wasted movement fell from **35.1% to 14.0%**, and the agent beat our handwritten baseline **50–0**.

Later, a higher-level planner became a bottleneck. Even when fed teachers' reconstructed investment schedules on 21 held-out games, it banked only about **55k**, against the teachers' **106k**. This diagnosed limitations of that executor's placement, labor, timing, and selling. We moved execution back into the network while retaining shadow-state accounting.

We also tried extensive PPO and self-play. A scratch run on the final-sized architecture reached **47M environment steps over 91 hours** without learning useful farming. One BC-initialized PPO branch improved its public rating from 1738.5 to 2322.0, but the local gain was insignificant and the ladder comparison included possible field drift.

The later BC chain overtook that branch. **No RL updates were applied to the final agent described here.**

## The tomato overlay

Our stronger BC agents still lost close games late. Across 94 losses from two versions, **62% were not behind at day 20**. On day 22, they averaged **0.9 tomato plants**, versus opponents' **7.9**.

A parallel LLM-selector experiment helped explore crop-timing changes. We distilled its useful tomato decision into deterministic code, matching **140/140 tested LLM decisions**.

The final rule replaced planned carrot-seed purchases with tomato seed on **engine days 16–19**, provided:

- Tomato price was at least 1.25 times base price and an unlocked shop bought tomatoes.
- Plants plus held seeds stayed within eight per tomato-buying shop.
- At least 300 coins remained after purchase.

Tomatoes produce four times before decaying, making planting time important for the late-season shortage.

The overlay also directed carried goods toward the shed during the final 20 steps and added final-step sales. Against the plain base on **96 fresh seeds, both seats**, with five rotating opponents, the complete overlay gained:

| Metric | Paired improvement, 95% CI |
| --- | ---: |
| Panel score | **+0.130 [0.072, 0.189]** |
| Final bank | **+1,456 [688, 2,224]** |

Its standalone leaderboard contribution remained unresolved: the plain control was retired before the private tournament. The evidence for this improvement is the paired local test.

## Evaluation and deployment

We selected checkpoints through **full greedy games**, using matched seeds, seats, and opponents, separate development and confirmation bands, and confidence intervals over seeds. External opponents and same-recipe retrains helped expose overfitting and training noise.

Offline accuracy could improve while play remained poor. One stage raised turn-exact accuracy from **0.085 to 0.248** without winning a game against the reference.

Deployment used a **NumPy policy in one file**, approximately 24.5 MB zipped. Export checks reproduced **2,876/2,876 action turns** between PyTorch and NumPy. Quiet-host p99 inference latency was approximately **0.28–0.29 seconds**.

We trained on an RTX 3090 Ti and a machine with four GTX 1080 Ti cards. Broad pretraining took about 12 hours; later 6,000-update fine-tunes took about 50 minutes on the four-card machine.

The experiments we would prioritize earlier next time are teacher-version audits, executor tests with true teacher targets, and full-game comparisons of proposed failure fixes. Those diagnostics repeatedly changed where we spent our effort.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to the hosts and all teams sharing public replays, especially DSM, DECEM, and yuto083 for the final specialist demonstrations. Earlier stages also benefited from other public leaders. Our separate scripted-baseline line used Ahmed Berat Ozer's V43 agent, shared through sdy623's notebook under Apache-2.0.

# Overview

My solution used heuristics and search, without machine learning. It combined an opening book derived from top players' public replays with daily planning based mainly on simulated annealing and beam search. For the final submission, the opening book came from the public replays of **M & M & P & Q**.

The [submission notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/mtmrs1/32nd-place-solution-opening-book-heuristics) explains the solution in detail. The diagram below, created with Claude Opus 5.5 based on that notebook, summarizes the agent's architecture. Here, I will focus on how I approached the competition and developed the agent.

# From replay-based strategies to AI-driven heuristic development

When I first looked into this competition, building an agent that could adapt to the game state seemed very difficult. Submitted agents' actions were also exposed through public replays. Some discussions suggested that there might be little room for improvement beyond copying strong fixed scenarios and making small modifications. Initially, I shared that view.

I started with [Three-Day Shop Router](https://www.kaggle.com/code/yhay81/three-day-shop-router), the strongest public notebook I had found at the time. I asked GPT-6 Pro to improve it, and in a single chat turn, it produced a version that substantially outperformed the original in local matches.

That experiment convinced me to pursue an AI-driven approach to improving fixed scenarios and their surrounding heuristics. However, I thought that simply asking the model to keep improving the agent would eventually stall, so I continued to steer the direction of development.

One important turning point came when the AI proposed rebuilding the plan for the final day. This made me wonder whether the same idea could be applied on earlier days as well. That led to the final architecture: an opening book followed by daily replanning.

For the opening book, I moved from public notebooks to collecting public replays that were both strong and easy to reuse as opening routines. I used DECEM and DSM replays for much of development. Near the end of the competition, I updated the book with M & M & P & Q replays.

The approach worked better than I had initially expected. On September 23, one week before the submission deadline, my agent reached third place on the public leaderboard.

Other participants kept improving their agents, though, and I ended up finishing **32nd with a silver medal**.

# Notes on working with AI

I mainly used GPT-6 Pro through the ChatGPT Pro 5x plan. Among the models I tried, it stood out for this kind of work. Toward the end of the competition, however, I felt that its performance had declined, and I saw other users reporting similar experiences. This was difficult to assess quantitatively, but it made it harder to make steady progress.

I also used Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol with xhigh reasoning, partly because of usage limits.

Codex and Work had very restrictive usage limits, while chat was unlimited except for Pro mode. I therefore set up GitHub Actions so ChatGPT could launch cloud instances with many CPU cores and run large batches of matches between agent versions directly from the chat interface.

*I drafted this writeup in Japanese, my native language, then used GPT-6.1-Sol to translate it into English and polish the wording and formatting. I reviewed and edited the English version before publishing it.*

text:
A good farm layout is only the beginning of a Kaggriculture strategy. Animals need feed, harvests need transport, workers need to arrive at the right time, and products need to reach the market. A policy can make a sensible choice at every individual station and still fail to run the farm as a whole.

Our approach is to learn that complete policy from replays. A single **22.4-million-parameter network** predicts the farmer's command, the hired workers' commands, and an ordered list of market instructions. The released agent uses supervised behavior cloning, with a small final-turn liquidation rule. It does not choose among hand-written farming plans.

The central design separates three kinds of coordination: **memory across turns, attention between workers, and sequential decoding between market orders**. This article explains why those mechanisms are useful, how to construct their training problem, and how to turn the trained network into an agent. The [companion repository](https://github.com/zhuzhirui2005/Kaggriculture-Replay-Agent) includes the pretrained checkpoint and the data, training, and inference code.

## A policy that remembers and coordinates

Imagine a worker arriving at storage. Is it finishing a harvest delivery, starting a feeding trip, or collecting an animal for a new pasture? Position alone cannot answer that question. Inventory and the previous command help, but a multi-turn job may need more context.

Now imagine two workers standing on different empty tiles, both ready to plant wheat. Each action looks reasonable in isolation. If the farm has only one wheat seed, the pair cannot both succeed.

These are different problems. The first calls for a representation of the recent trajectory; the second calls for communication and shared-resource accounting. Treating them separately makes the architecture easier to reason about.

*Figure 1. Three kinds of coordination. GRUs carry information across turns; attention exchanges information within the current turn; a separate GRU generates market orders in sequence. The farming illustrations are schematic.*

### Encode both the local job and the whole economy

The input has a spatial part and an economic part. A **52 × 10 × 10** tensor represents both publicly visible farms in own-player-first order, including tile states, crops, animals, worker occupancy, and coordinates. A **114-dimensional** feature vector describes time, finances, expansion, shop availability, market prices and stocks, observed market changes, and our private inventory. Large counts use scaled inverse-hyperbolic-sine transforms so that small quantities remain distinguishable.

A residual CNN encodes the board. One path summarizes it into a farm-wide context; another gathers the encoded cell beneath each worker. Worker features then add inventory, a within-day slot embedding, and the previous command and quantity. Previous market instructions also contribute to the shared context through pooled embeddings.

This representation exposes the opponent's public production without exposing their private storage. Future shop unlocks and hidden world information are not inputs.

### Remember a day's work, then coordinate the current turn

A shared GRU carries farm-wide history, while a shared-parameter GRU maintains a separate state for each worker. Both use 256-dimensional hidden states and reset at day boundaries, matching the replacement of hired workers. This gives the model capacity to learn task continuity without requiring an explicit task queue.

Two attention layers then operate on the current context token and worker tokens. They let a worker's representation incorporate what other workers are positioned to do. Absent workers are masked. This is **same-turn attention**, not attention over future replay frames.

| Component                         | Released configuration                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Board encoder                     | 192 channels, three residual convolutional blocks            |
| Shared and worker representations | 768 dimensions; up to 32 actors including the farmer         |
| Daily recurrent memory            | Shared and per-worker GRUs, each with 256 hidden units       |
| Worker attention                  | Two layers, four heads, 1,536-dimensional feedforward layers |
| Market decoder                    | 768-dimensional GRU; at most ten orders                      |

### Give different demonstrations a consistent policy mode

Replays contain different, sometimes incompatible ways to play. One demonstrator may commit labor to animals where another would expand crop production. Asking an unconditional model to imitate both can leave the decision ambiguous.

A learned **style embedding** provides a condition on our own policy. The same network shares spatial, economic, and execution knowledge across styles, while the embedding distinguishes their behavior. At inference, one style is fixed for the entire game; the published default is named `default`. It is not an opponent classifier, and the agent does not switch styles in response to a guessed opponent identity.

## Turn predictions into a structured action

Rather than flattening an entire turn into one enormous category, the model decomposes it into commands, quantities, and an ordered market sequence.

Workers have **44 command tokens**. Crop or item identity is part of the relevant command token, and a command-conditioned head predicts quantities from 0 to 100 where applicable. This avoids asking an independent quantity head to choose a number before knowing what operation it belongs to.

Local masks remove obviously infeasible choices, but must respect the environment's execution order. For example, an earlier worker may build a pasture before a later worker places an animal there. Rejecting placement solely because there was no pasture at the start of the turn would remove a valid collaboration.

Shared seeds need an additional mechanism. Worker scores are computed together, but planting choices are resolved in execution order. Selecting a planting command consumes that crop's quota; later workers can no longer select it once the quota is exhausted. This is a limited, explicit resource constraint—not a fully autoregressive worker policy or a general joint-action planner.

*Figure 2. Two independent examples. A shared seed quota prevents duplicate consumption; an ordered market decoder represents dependencies between instructions. The examples illustrate decoding, not a recorded game.*

Market instructions form a different sequence. A **23-token vocabulary** covers supported purchases, sales, hiring, expansion, and an end marker. Starting from the shared context after attention, a GRU generates each order and its quantity, then conditions the next order on that choice. A sale followed by a purchase is therefore distinguishable from an unordered pair of intentions.

Training uses the demonstrated market prefix; deployment feeds back the model's own chosen prefix and uses greedy decoding. The worker and market branches share representations, but the market decoder does not explicitly receive the worker commands just selected for that turn.

## Make replays into the right learning problem

The most important preprocessing detail is easy to miss: **the action stored in replay record `t + 1` belongs with observation `t`**. It is the command that led out of the current observation, not an instruction chosen after seeing the next state. An off-by-one error can still produce a falling loss while teaching the wrong mapping.

For each selected player, the processor merges the public observation with that player's private observation and constructs the action target. The targets imitate submitted commands rather than reconstructing every action the engine ultimately executed. Known infeasible labels are excluded. In particular, when a demonstrated turn requests more planting of a crop than the available seeds allow, its planting labels for that crop are excluded rather than teaching the conflict.

Whole episodes are assigned to train, validation, or test **before** sampling sequences. Both seats stay in the same partition: the two perspectives of one game are not independent examples. The implementation uses a stable episode-ID hash for an approximately 80/10/10 split.

*Figure 3. Future replay information can provide training targets without becoming a policy input. Record alignment and episode-level splitting are part of the learning problem, not just file handling.*

Training samples 24-frame days, initializes recurrent memory to zero, and backpropagates through the day's sequence. The final short day is padded, with padded action and intent labels ignored. Compressed per-seat arrays provide a portable intermediate format; read-only memory-mapped caches avoid repeatedly decompressing trajectories during training.

### Teach what a route is for

An action label such as `EAST` says little about the job behind the movement. Consider a route that goes east, east, north, then feeds an animal. In addition to predicting the immediate command, auxiliary heads learn the destination cell and the work command the route is leading toward.

The target is the nearest non-movement, non-pass action within the current-to-next-twelve-turn window, without crossing a day boundary. These intent labels come from replay supervision. At inference, they are not fed into a separate path planner.

A scalar auxiliary head predicts the remaining change in cash margin, scaled by 10,000, plus twice the sign of the final margin. It supplies another training signal about the trajectory's outcome; deployment does not use it for action search.

The combined objective is:

```text
L = L_worker + 0.5 L_worker_quantity
  + L_market + 0.5 L_market_quantity
  + 0.2 L_goal_cell + 0.2 L_goal_command
  + 0.1 L_return
```

Action and intent terms use cross-entropy; the return term uses Smooth L1. Worker `PASS` receives weight 0.5, while planting, building, placement, pickup, and digging receive weight 2. Other worker commands receive weight 1. Missing actors, inapplicable quantities, and excluded labels do not contribute to their respective losses.

### Avoid depending on perfect demonstration history

During training, the preceding commands usually come from a demonstrator. During play, they come from the model itself. That difference matters as soon as the learner makes a mistake.

We randomly erase 15% of previous worker command/quantity pairs. Previous market histories are erased as whole prefixes with the same probability. The current observation and target action remain unchanged. The intended effect is to make action history useful without making a clean teacher prefix indispensable.

This does not solve the full distribution-shift problem: erasing history does not create the new board states caused by the learner's errors. Full-game testing remains necessary.

## A practical training recipe

The training code supports both learning from scratch and continuing from the released checkpoint. Continuation can mix new demonstrations with older rehearsal data, with a default 70/30 ratio when both are present. New styles are sampled uniformly before choosing a trajectory and a day, so a prolific source does not dominate simply by supplying more replay files.

| Setting                 | Reference recipe                             |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Optimizer               | AdamW, weight decay `1e-4`                   |
| Learning rate           | `1e-4` from scratch; `1e-5` for continuation |
| Sequence unit           | One 24-frame day                             |
| Gradient norm clipping  | 1                                            |
| CUDA precision          | bfloat16 forward computation                 |
| History erasure         | 15%                                          |
| New / rehearsal mixture | 70% / 30%, when both groups are available    |

These are reproducible starting settings, not a claim that each is independently optimal.

The implementation batches board encoding across frames, advances recurrent states chronologically, then batches same-turn attention and action heads. Read-only memory mapping lets training processes share prepared data without loading separate copies into RAM.

For multi-GPU training, each process receives a slice of the global day batch. Loss normalization uses globally summed target weights: class weights for worker commands, and valid-label counts for unweighted heads. Because worker counts and applicable quantities vary, averaging each GPU's local mean would give sparse and dense batches the wrong relative influence.

The short reproduction path is:

1. Prepare complete replays with stable episode IDs, selected seats, and consistent style labels using `tools.data prepare`.
2. Build memory-mapped arrays with `tools.data cache`.
3. Train with `tools.train`, optionally warm-starting from `weights/model.pt`; use `torchrun` for distributed training.
4. Test frozen checkpoints in complete games, then build the runtime archive with `tools.package`.

The repository README gives the commands and manifest format.

## Deploy the policy you actually evaluate

The runtime loads one checkpoint, fixes one style, carries daily memory, and decodes greedily on CPU. Its history records the actions actually returned to the environment. Repeated calls on the same observation do not advance recurrent memory twice. Training utilities and replay data are not part of the submission package.

One narrow economic rule remains outside the network: **final-turn liquidation**. On the last actionable turn, it projects the immediate effects of our worker commands, then adds or extends sales of products available in storage. Already requested sales and the market-order limit are respected. The original worker commands are unchanged.

This addresses a finite-horizon mismatch: inventory useful for tomorrow has no production value when there is no tomorrow. The rule does not intervene in ordinary production, sell goods that remain in a worker's hands, or replace earlier plans. With scarce order slots, it uses current price times quantity to prioritize remaining products, rather than searching for an optimal final transaction sequence.

The model and this rule must be evaluated together. Adding a postprocessor after measuring a checkpoint means deploying a different policy.

## What to take away

Replay prediction and competitive strength answer different questions. Held-out loss can reveal alignment errors, missing features, or difficult action classes. Complete games reveal whether individually plausible decisions form a working farm. Use fresh worlds and both seats, prioritize win rate, keep ties visible, and inspect repeated failure patterns rather than choosing a model on a few extreme score margins.

Behavior cloning also has a ceiling: it approximates observed decisions, encounters states absent from its demonstrations, and can compound its own errors. The explanations above motivate the architecture; they are not controlled ablations assigning a win-rate gain to each component.

The transferable idea is to make the **structure of the execution problem** visible to learning. Local spatial features describe the job, daily memory supplies continuity, attention connects workers, and structured decoding handles commands and shared resources. This turns replay imitation from isolated action prediction into a practical way to learn how to run the whole farm.

Hi Kagglers! 👋

In synthetic tabular competitions like S6E10 (CTGAN-generated), the natural temptation is to **blindly expand features**—generating hundreds of interaction terms, target encodings, frequency tables, and statistical aggregations.

Inspired by several insightful discussions in our community, I conducted a **rigorous 5-fold scientific ablation study** across 4 popular candidate feature expansion modules (136 candidate features in total). The empirical results challenged standard intuition and exposed what we term the **"Feature Dilution Effect" in GBDT models**—blindly adding features actually degraded out-of-fold generalization!

Today, I am open-sourcing our complete, self-contained **15-fold GPU tree pipeline (Pure Standalone Tree Stack: Public LB 0.96114)**, and sharing how combining this clean baseline with external foundation models pushed our overall **OOF AUC to 0.96238**.

---

### 🙏 1. Standing on the Shoulders of Giants (Credits & Gratitude)

This work was made possible thanks to ideas shared openly by the community. Huge shout-out to:
- **@giannhsstamelias**: For discovering that in ordinal ratings, a score of `0` is **NOT** extreme dissatisfaction, but rather a structural **"Not Applicable / Unexperienced (N/A)"** flag.
- **@Shelton Wang**: For the inspiring breakdown of high-signal cross-domain interactions for CatBoost (`Class` / `Type of Travel` × Service Ratings).
- **@Sachith7**: For highlighting the immense value of using the uncorrupted original airline dataset as a Super Teacher prior.
- **@Chris Deotte**: For open-sourcing the incredible dataset of 11 Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) out-of-fold predictions.

---

### 🚨 2. The Great Ablation: Why 136 Candidate Features Hurt CV

Starting from a lean 84D baseline (LightGBM 5-Fold OOF AUC: `0.960262`), we independently evaluated 4 candidate expansion modules:

| Feature Expansion Module | Extra Dims | 5-Fold OOF AUC | Net Delta ($\Delta$ vs Base) | Conclusion |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Clean 84D Core** | **-** | **`0.960262`** | **Reference** | **Optimal Information Density** |
| `copy1_route` (Flight distance & rating residual routes) | +41 | `0.959788` | **-0.000474** 🔻 | Significant Drop |
| `copy2_org` (Original dataset marginal lookup tables) | +21 | `0.960093` | **-0.000169** 🔻 | Negative Contribution |
| `copy3_freq` (Category frequency encoding tables) | +42 | `0.960017` | **-0.000245** 🔻 | Negative Contribution |
| `copy4_digit` (Modulo math & first/last digit hashes) | +32 | `0.959896` | **-0.000366** 🔻 | Significant Drop |

Even when extracting standalone features with **univariate AUC > 0.80**, injecting them into the baseline still degraded the CV score.

**Why does this happen? (The Feature Dilution Effect)**
1. **Subsampling Dilution (`colsample_bytree = 0.7`)**: Trees sample a random subset of features for each tree. Redundant or noisy variants reduce the probability of selecting truly critical drivers (such as the `Super Teacher` score and key cross-interactions).
2. **Split Competition**: Decision trees make greedy splits. Correlated derivatives compete for split variance, splintering clean decision boundaries into fragmented sub-trees and causing subtle leaf-level overfitting.

**Engineering Decision**: We decisively **pruned all 136 candidate features** and eliminated 18 redundant baseline columns, locking our core feature space at **84 pure dimensions**.

---

### 💡 3. From Clean 15-Fold Tree Baseline (LB 0.96114) to Orthogonal Ensemble (OOF 0.96238)

Our solution architecture follows a two-stage strategy:

#### Stage 1: The Self-Contained 15-Fold GPU Tree Baseline (Open-Sourced Code)
- Built on the pruned 84D feature space (treating zeros as NaN for horizontal aggregates, cross-interactions, cognitive expectation gaps, and an uncorrupted Super Teacher prior).
- Scaled from 5-fold (80% train) to **15-fold (93.3% train, ~653k rows/fold)**.
- 15-fold parallel training on LightGBM + XGBoost + CatBoost drastically shrinks prediction variance.
- **Score**: Without blending any external public predictions, this pure tree stack hits **Public LB 0.96114**.

#### Stage 2: Orthogonal Fusion with Tabular Foundation Models
- Many high-scoring community blends (0.9618+) are heavy blends of shared public files that suffer from high mutual correlation ($\rho > 0.9999$).
- Because our 15-fold 84D tree model was trained strictly independently, its errors are **genuinely orthogonal** to neural/transformer representations.
- By stacking our 15-fold predictions with **@Chris Deotte's 11 Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs)** using an L2-regularized Logistic Regression ($C=0.003$) in logit space:
  $$z = \ln \left( \frac{p}{1 - p} \right)$$
  our overall ensemble OOF AUC surged to **`0.96238`**!

---

### 📦 Full Open-Source Reproducible Pipeline

The complete, end-to-end 15-fold GPU training and feature construction notebook is fully public and executable:

text:
Code, weights and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/KawattaTaido/kaggriculture-release (CC BY 4.0).

Thank you to the organizers for hosting this competition.

## 1. Summary

The agent is **one policy network** (21.8M parameters, JAX/Flax), with no search and no
hand-written planner. It is trained in two steps:

1. **Behavior cloning (BC)** on the most recent leaderboard games: 2,380 episodes from
   the last four days before the final submission, using both seats.
2. **PPO** (≈370M environment steps, ≈19 h on one RTX 5090). In half of the games the
   agent plays itself. In the other half it plays one opponent from a small pool: two
   past generations of itself, or a **recording of a real LB agent** replayed move by move.

Three things mattered most:

- **The action representation follows the game.** Each worker unit *points at a target
  tile*, and the market head outputs *a quantity per item*.
- **The strength of the BC starting point, driven by fresh LB data.** A new day of LB
  games was released every morning, and rebuilding the BC teachers from the latest days
  made the model stronger almost every time. Imitating top agents was the cheapest large gain (Section 4).
- **Model size.** Making the network wider kept improving the results; the last two
  widenings took it to 11.96M and then 21.83M parameters. The gain does not show in BC;
  it shows only after PPO (Section 4).

At a glance:

- **Most important inputs**: the own-farm map with plant and animal states, market
  prices, stocks and price impact, the money and stock of both players, and estimates of
  the opponent's hidden barn and of when the opponent will deliver.
- **Tools**:
  - JAX / Flax / Optax for the network and PPO; a JAX port of the environment runs all
    PPO rollouts on the GPU.
  - Rust (PyO3) for the game rules, legal-action masks and observation features. The
    same compiled extension is used in training and in the submission.
  - `kaggle-environments` as the reference implementation.
- **Training time** (one RTX 5090): ≈23 h from the release of the last day of LB data to the
  final weights; ≈3.5 h for the data and BC, ≈19 h for PPO.
- **Inference**: ≈18 ms per turn locally, greedy (argmax) decoding. No ensemble.

---

## 2. Features selection / engineering

The input is not a feature table but the game state, encoded into three tensors
(specification v12). Every feature is computed in Rust; a JAX implementation is checked
against it bit by bit, and replays of LB games verify both.

| Input | Shape | Content |
|---|---|---|
| map | 65 × 10 × 10 | own farm: tile type, crop, plant state (water, fertilizer, turns to maturity, expected yield), animal state, unit occupancy, **number of harvests left in the season** |
| global | 312 | time and phase one-hots, money, seeds, barn and carried stock, market prices / stocks / price impact, town demand, labor, land, recent history, expected supply, **estimated opponent stock and delivery timing**, stock in hand + barn |
| units | 24 × 25 (+ mask) | per worker: position, carried items, distance to the barn, … |

Most important, judged by what changed results when added or removed:

1. **Market state and price impact.** Selling moves the price; both players share one
   market, and the town buys only a fixed amount (≈206k per game in total over all
   items).
2. **Opponent estimates.** The opponent's barn is not observable, so its stock is
   estimated from public information (purchases, harvests, sales), together with when it
   will deliver. An auxiliary head that predicts the opponent's sales 1 and 24 turns ahead
   (loss weight 0.05) trains the same representation.
3. **Plant state, including the harvests left in the season.** Continuing crops
   (strawberry, tomato) are worth more when several harvests remain.

Feature selection and transformations:

- Features were added one hypothesis at a time and kept only if BC *and* PPO improved,
  judged by paired comparisons on the same boards.
- A map of the opponent's farm was removed (no effect). Two later specifications were not
  adopted because they lost after PPO (Section 4).

**External data**: none apart from the LB replays published through the Kaggle API (the
competition's own episodes).

## 3. Training methods

No ensembling; one network.

*Figure 1. Training pipeline. LB replays feed both behavior cloning and the "tape" slot of
the PPO opponent pool. Every 210 PPO iterations the KL teacher is replaced by the current
weights, and the current weights join the opponent pool.*

### Network (Figure 2)

*Figure 2. Network. The own-farm map is encoded by a ResNet and self-attention, the global
vector by an MLP, and the worker units attend to the board. Three heads produce unit
actions, market orders and value/auxiliary predictions. Every factor of every action is
masked by legal-action masks computed in Rust.*

| Part | Details |
|---|---|
| Map encoder | ResNet, 6 blocks, 96 channels, GroupNorm; FiLM conditioning on the global vector; 2 self-attention layers over the 100 tiles |
| Global encoder | MLP, hidden 512 → g (1024) |
| Unit encoder | 2 cross-attention layers from units to tiles, with a relative-position bias, then unit self-attention |
| **Unit head (pointer)** | per unit, autoregressive: operation, **target tile** (logit = query·tile key + learned function of distance / dx / dy / reservations of earlier units), argument, quantity. A unit on its target performs the operation; otherwise it moves one step along a fixed path. Targets are re-chosen every turn. A tile and operation already reserved by an earlier unit is masked, so units never duplicate work. |
| **Market head** | a turn's market action is a *quantity per item* (21 factors, 352 logits), decoded autoregressively in execution order by a 2-layer transformer over 14 item tokens. Budget and order-slot limits are tracked while decoding, so every sampled action is legal. The orders are then placed into the 10 order slots by a fixed rule: sells of items the opponent also holds come first, largest expected price drop first, because the environment processes the two players' slots alternately and earlier slots sell at higher prices. |
| Value / auxiliary | value head (final money difference), auxiliary heads (final money, win probability, opponent sales) |
| Size | 21.83M parameters; compute in bfloat16 |

**Legal-action masks** are computed in Rust and applied to every factor. Besides the
rules, they remove actions that are provably wasteful:

- market orders that are certainly loss-making or cannot fill;
- digging up a plant before harvest (continuing crops excepted);
- fertilizer that does not raise the yield;
- planting that cannot mature before the season ends;
- care on the last day;
- dropping items into a full barn.

Each mask was checked by replaying LB games, so it does not remove moves that top agents
actually play.

### Behavior cloning

- **Teachers**: 2,380 LB games of 2026-09-26..29 in which both players had a rating of at
  least 2,800, both seats (3.4M samples; 1,891 games for training, 489 held out).
- **Labels**: LB actions are projected onto the network's action representation (target
  tile for units, quantity per item for the market). A sell and a buy of the same item in
  the same turn are netted, and sells are budgeted against the barn *after* the unit
  actions of the turn.
- **Training**: 60k steps, batch 512, Adam with lr 3e-4 and a cosine schedule, gradient
  clip 1.0, auxiliary opponent-sales loss 0.05. Hold-out NLL 5.35 per sample (retrained model in the repository; the original BC checkpoint was lost).

### PPO

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Environment | JAX port, 64 games in parallel, whole 720-turn game in `lax.scan` on the GPU |
| Reward | final money difference / 30,000, terminal only; γ = λ = 1 |
| Update | clip 0.2, 2 epochs, 16 minibatches, entropy 0.02, value 0.5, auxiliary 0.1, grad norm 0.5, early stop on KL (0.003) |
| Learning rate | stage 1: 5e-5 for 420 iterations; stage 2: **1e-5** for 3,570 iterations |
| Kickstarting | KL to a teacher policy, coefficient 1.0. The teacher starts as the BC model and is **replaced by the current weights every 210 iterations** ("segments"). |
| Opponents | 50% self-play; 50% one of a pool of 3: two past generations (pushed every 210 iterations) and one **LB tape** |
| TV guard | after each update, if the 90th percentile over games of the change in action probabilities (total variation) at any turn exceeds 0.5, the update is shrunk to ½ or ¼ |

**LB tape opponent.** One pool slot replays a recorded LB agent. The recordings come from
800 games: 657 LB games of 2026-09-25..28 (both ratings ≥ 2,800) and 143 LB games that our earlier submissions lost. A
recording is open-loop, so two things are aligned with the original game:

- **Randomness.** The tape seat's random events (weeds, the shop unlock order) follow the
  recording.
- **Market fills.** For every order of the recorded player, the number of units that
  filled on the LB is precomputed. The replay stops at that number, and missing money is
  lent and subtracted at the end.

Without this alignment, a difference of a few coins on day 0 makes the tape's first
purchases fail, and in about 30% of games the opponent collapses. Opponents are sampled
per team, and teams that are harder to beat are drawn more often.

*Figure 3. During PPO training, the win rate against the recorded LB agents (the tape
slot of the pool) rose from 0.53 to ≈0.88.*

## 4. Interesting findings

**What mattered most**

1. **Fresh BC teachers.** A new day of LB games was released every morning, and rebuilding
   the BC teachers from the latest four days made the model stronger almost every time.
   This was the cheapest large gain. On one model
   generation it raised the win rate against a strong public rule-based agent from 0.835
   to 0.993.
2. **An action representation that matches the game**: pointing at tiles instead of
   choosing move directions, quantities per item instead of a fixed list of order slots,
   and sell budgets counted on the real barn.
3. **Model size, which shows up in PPO, not in BC.** Every widening of the network improved
   the final result. Wider fully connected layers barely changed the BC hold-out NLL
   (−0.04) and lost BC-vs-BC games. At the same PPO step count, however, they raised the
   win rate against tapes from 0.454 to 0.589.
4. **Realistic recorded opponents.** Self-play alone never meets some LB behaviors, such
   as selling in the same turn as a delivery or replanting late. The tapes only helped
   once randomness and fills were aligned (Section 3).
5. **A low learning rate for long PPO runs.** At 5e-5 the run stopped improving after
   about 40M steps. Restarting at 1e-5:
   - lowered the clipped fraction from 0.26 to 0.09;
   - gained +355 money against held-out LB tapes in two seeds;
   - won head-to-head (0.56 and 0.69);
   - kept improving for the remaining 3,500 iterations (Figure 3).
6. **Guarding against "opening flips".** A single ordinary-sized update sometimes flipped
   the near-deterministic opening purchases (for example buying 3 geese on turn 1). Each
   flip sent the policy into another strategy. A KL measured on sampled actions cannot
   see this (≈3e-5 on average). The per-turn TV guard removed all such spikes in a
   verification run, at a cost of +9% time per iteration.

**Relationships in the game**

- **Fixed demand.** The town buys a fixed amount per game (≈206k in total), and the two
  players' sales nearly saturate it, so taking the opponent's share is the shortest way
  to win.
- **Shared market.** When our money rose by 1,000, the opponent's rose by 690–790, through
  the shared market. Maximizing our own money and maximizing the win rate are therefore
  different objectives. The PPO reward is the money *difference*.
- **One loss-making action.** A single legal but certainly loss-making action (for
  example an animal that cannot pay back before the end) is enough to make PPO suppress
  all spending, including planting. Masking provable losses was a prerequisite for
  learning.

**Tried and not adopted** (each lost in paired evaluation):

- day-level planners and solvers for the workforce (timed out on Kaggle or lost
  head-to-head);
- local search over the policy's actions;
- a calendar one-hot plus "next land" features, and opponent-unit cross-attention (both
  better in BC, both worse after PPO);
- a weaker kickstart (0.3);

## 5. Simple features and methods

- **Simplest useful model**: the BC model alone, with the same network and inputs and
  no PPO. It already plays a complete, sensible economy because it imitates recent top
  LB agents, and it needs no long training (≈3.5 h on an RTX 5090, data preparation included).
- **Most important step**: PPO starting from BC. Figure 3 shows the gain against recorded
  LB agents during training. Most of the improvement comes in the first ≈2,000
  iterations (≈10 h on an RTX 5090).
- **Smaller input subsets** were not evaluated systematically. The input is the encoded
  game state rather than a hand-made feature table, so it does not reduce to a short list
  of features.

## 6. Model execution time

| | Time |
|---|---|
| LB data download, BC dataset and BC training (60k steps) | ≈3.5 h |
| PPO stage 1 (420 iterations) | ≈2.2 h |
| PPO stage 2 (3,570 iterations) | ≈17 h |
| Total | ≈23 h on one RTX 5090 (≈17 s per PPO iteration) |
| Prediction | ≈18 ms per turn locally; about 35 ms per turn and ≈35 s for the first turn (JIT compilation) on Kaggle's runtime, measured on an earlier submission. A game has 720 turns. |
| Simplified model (BC only) | training ≈3.5 h; prediction as above |
