text:
**Final result: 573rd of 10,148 (top 5.6%), a bronze-range finish.** On the live ladder it ended 481st, inside silver; the final Bradley-Terry ranking over all two weeks of post-deadline games placed it 573rd. No trained model: the agent is a hand-written planner. I built it over eight weeks and it took five separate attempts to get there. This is the story of those attempts, how the final agent plays, and the things I'd do differently.

Thanks to the organizers for a wonderful game, and to everyone whose replays, notebooks and write-ups taught me something. Credits are at the end.

## Five attempts in eight weeks

I treated this as a learning project.  Along the way, I ran into brick walls and had to restart from scratch four times.  Each time, though, I solved new problems and for the most part the agent improved, in some areas if not in others.  By the final submission deadline I had an agent I was pretty happy with, although it wound up just shy of the silver medal I had been hoping for.  

| Attempt                                                               | Dates           | Best rating                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------- |
| 1. A planner tuned by an evolution strategy using CMA-ES              | Aug 4 – Aug 21  | 879                             |
| 2. Attempting to remove the genome from the original code base        | Aug 21 – Sep 1  | 1,050                           |
| 3. Imitation Learning, an preliminary first attempt                   | Aug 27 – Aug 29 | 850                             |
| 4. A fresh start: rollout search over the season                      | Sep 1 – Sep 22  | 1,354                           |
| 5. Another fresh start: copy the best players boards with my executor | Sep 22 – Sep 30 | **2,109** (final ladder rating) |

Ratings from different weeks aren't really comparable, because the field kept getting stronger. Rank tells the story better: top 57% in mid-August, top 31% in mid-September, top 5.6% at the end.

All of my attempts separated the agent into a planner and an executor.  The planner made decisions, the executor ran the farm, hired workers, assigned them tasks, planned routes, and controlled sales.  

**Attempt 1** started with my idea of tuning a planner's weights by an evolution strategy.  Using a "genome" of about 30 elements, the idea was to tune that genome through CMA-ES. The executor improved quickly through ordinary design work. CMA-ES never helped: it tuned the wrong things, mutated the elements of the genome too slowly, and wasn't improving on the ladder. I tried to proceed by freezing the genome and working around it, but that was too limiting.  When I first attempted to remove the genome, the agent collapsed. The genome had been masking deep-seated issues in the executor.  The best rating during this period was 879.

**Attempt 2** was an trying to retain the existing code, remove the genome, and fix the underlying issues.  This worked for a while, but ultimately the design was not what I would build from scratch.  Final rating was 1,050.

For **Attempt 3** I trained a model to imitate the top of field's shared opening. It reached 99.5% accuracy on that opening, but the opening left the ladder within days, and its advice was neutral in live play.  I abandoned this attempt, perhaps too early, thinking I lacked the hardware to implement something like PPO on top of the imitation learning I was doing.  

**Attempt 4** started from scratch on 1 September. I built a new planner and a new executor.  This time the planner would use full rollout search over the rest of the season over a number of different simulated towns to see which candidate plans did best on average.  Each morning it ran its rollouts and recommended new actions.  The executor would take those plans and implement them.  It passed attempt 2 within four days, peaked around 1,370 a week later, and then stalled for a week. This approach had two significant limitations.  The first was compute: in python, the planner was slow.  It was trying to choose between 8 or so candidate plans by simulating full seasons and opponent reactions across multiple different towns.  It made better choices with more compute available, but at kaggle speeds with the 1s per turn / 60 s time bank, it was limited in how many plans and rollouts it could handle.  

The second limitation was related to compute: its vocabulary was limited.  It could not fully express all the different plans that might be possible, and so had to use generalizations.  It would leave a few tiles empty here or there because it had calculated, (e.g.) that 12 strawberry plants in the NE quadrant were a good idea, but didn't have the vocabulary to express that the remaining three tiles should be wheat.  Evaluating more candidate plans solved the limitation, but vastly exceeded the compute budget.  I tried to patch over these planning deficiencies with different heuristics in the executor (if a tile isn't specified by the planner, plant wheat, if no new decision is made, harvest and replant same crop, etc.) but this was eventually too cumbersome to work with.  So many different rules were injected into different pieces of the executor that were really planning rules, I decided to scrap it all and start over again.

**Attempt 5** started from scratch on 22 September with eight days left, and became the final agent.

## How the final agent plays

For the final attempt I wanted a fixed opening, and then instead of a rollout planner use the crop / animal choices from a top competitor, run through my own executor.  

**Days 0-6: someone else's opening.** Vadim Vasilenko played nearly the same opening in all 152 of his games I downloaded. I turned those games into a lookup table: in any situation Vadim reached, do what he did. That means a few melons, early cows and sheep, more animals over days 2-5, and spending down to almost nothing by day 6. If the game drifts somewhere Vadim never went, the planner takes over.

An early version replayed one of DSM's games move for move. It broke whenever my cash differed from his by even a few coins, which happened whenever the opponent bought wheat in the same turn. The table fixed that, because Vadim's own play already adapted to what he had.

**The melon race.** If the opponent planted ten or more melons on day 0, it fertilizes its own day-0 melons so they're ripe at dawn on day 10. Then it harvests and sells them before the opponent's melons crash the price.  If the opponent wasn't that heavy into melons, it could wait a few turns before getting its own to market.  

**Days 6-12: building the farm.** It buys a second quadrant on day 6 and a third on day 9, and never a fourth. Each quadrant is steered toward the farm Vadim had built by days 9 and 13 in towns with the same shops. The opening and those targets only worked together. Vadim's opening with someone else's build targets lost, and so did the reverse. Together they were worth about 5,900 coins a game in head-to-head tests, the largest single gain of the project.

**Days 13-28: the working farm.** Crop counts per quadrant follow what DSM grew in towns with similar shops. On top of that:
- Fertilized wheat is harvested at its best yield per day, not its maximum.
- Spent strawberries and tomatoes are dug up and replanted in the same visit.
- Six sheep are added for each yarn store that opens late.
- It hires 11 hands, and 12 from day 22. The twelfth hand costs about what it earns, but its output lowers the opponent's prices.
- From day 27 it feeds animals only when their remaining output pays for the feed.

**Every morning: routes.** It plans a route for every hand, sweeping jobs by direction around the shed and filling them in by value per turn. From day 13 it spends about a second shortening those routes. During the day, an idle hand takes over any job it can reach before the hand assigned to it.

**Day 29: planned exactly.** The last day has no future to worry about, so it's fully deterministic. The agent plans the whole crew's last day on the game's exact rules, with a search using about half its remaining time bank. It hires the last two hands only if the plan says they pay. A separate test showed every crop on a typical last-day board can be harvested and sold with about an hour to spare. My earlier agents were leaving 5-20 units in the field.

## Labor and routing: five attempts at the same problem

The hardest problem in this game isn't what to plant. It's getting a dozen workers through a few hundred jobs a day when each one does one action per turn, walks one tile per turn, and has to fetch feed and drop produce at a four-tile shed. Every attempt attacked it differently.

**Attempt 1: from auctions to owned days.** The first version re-scored every job every turn and gave each worker the best one, a fresh auction each turn. Workers abandoned errands halfway when something shinier appeared, and five different bugs turned out to be one disease: no decision could see what the others had already claimed. The fix was giving each worker its jobs for the whole day. Animal escapes went from about 2 a game to zero. A second rework sized the crew by costing the actual day plan, built routes by cheapest insertion, and executed them in deadline order. A hard-coded 15% "route slack" constant was quietly standing in for execution friction I hadn't yet measured, and the genome tuned around it.

**Attempt 2: every delivery as a chain with a deadline.** This design treated each product as a chain: produce, carry, return, drop, sell. A chain counts only if every step fits before its deadline. Animal care became atomic visit bundles; later, every published route task became a hard promise, with every planned task required to be executed. The approach was principled but heavy. Its last build inserted jobs into routes with a quadratic search, 97.6 million calls in one dawn, and ran out of Kaggle's time bank in 12 of 32 games. After that, every remaining step was a forced pass.

**Attempt 4: an exact executor inside every simulation.** Here the executor compiled the day's commitments into routes and dry-ran them under the engine's exact rules. Anything that wouldn't complete was dropped by value until every route finished, and crew size was found by binary search. Routing was crew-aware Clarke-Wright savings plus 2-opt. It was genuinely efficient: 0.82-0.94 moves per useful action, about what the top agents managed. But the planner scored candidate plans by simulating the rest of the season, and every simulation ran this executor. Compiling routes was about 77% of a simulation's cost. Any change that made the farm do more work per day made the simulations slower, so fewer fit in Kaggle's budget. This executor ran well when the planner was leaving empty tiles dotted around the farm, but patching that defect exposed the weakness of the labor routing.  It could handle 60ish occupied tiles well, but a full 75 and it broke down and important jobs started getting missed.  

**Attempt 5: one dawn plan, then cheap repairs.** The final agent plans once a day and keeps the planning out of any simulation:
- **Petal routes.** At hour 1, when the hired hands arrive, it sweeps the day's must-do tiles by angle around the shed and cuts the sweep into one "petal" per worker, sized to that worker's turns. It tries 12 starting angles and keeps the best, then orders each petal by nearest neighbour and 2-opt.
- **Prize-collecting.** Every visit and every drop carries a value in coins. Optional jobs go into a route only if they earn enough per extra turn.
- **Exact supplies.** Feed wheat is allocated route by route, so a worker never arrives at an animal without it. Fertilizer is collected from the animals on the way instead of fetched from the shed, which cut shed trips from 18 a day to 15 and was worth about 1,400 coins a game.
- **Repairs during the day.** A worker with nothing left takes over a job it can reach before the worker assigned to it.

The efficiency metrics I used throughout came from observing and measuring DSM's farm from replays. Late in the game his hands made about 148 productive actions a day to my 134-137. Most of the gap was shed trips: he made about 6 a day, I made about 13. His animals sat beside his wheat, so his hands fed what they just harvested. I closed part of that by copying his layout, never all of it.
## Spending the time bank: what got us into the top 6%

Kaggle gives each agent 1 second per turn plus a 60-second bank for the whole game. The early attempts learned to fear the bank: Attempt 2 lost a build to running it dry, and Attempt 4's season simulations never fit. By the last week my agent was using almost none of it: mostly under 0.1 seconds a turn, plus about 4 seconds to load its data tables. Two late changes spent it, and both landed in the final pair.

**1. The last day, planned exactly ** I asked a simple question while watching replays: is it even possible to harvest and sell everything on the last day? I wrote a solver, separate from the agent, that searches the whole crew's last-day plans on the engine's exact rules. Its moves are insertion, relocation, 2-opt, swaps, toggling water-before-harvest, and inserting drops. It runs simulated annealing with restarts. The answer: yes, with about an hour to spare, and 9-11 workers are enough on most boards. My agent's heuristic last day was leaving 5-20 units in the field.

On the last day nothing can surprise you. No weeds appear during the day, crops decay by a fixed rule, and the opponent can't touch your farm. So the plan can be computed and then executed action by action. The agent does exactly that:
- At hour 0 it hires 10 workers and searches with **half the remaining bank**.
- At hour 1 it decides whether the 11th and 12th workers pay for themselves, and searches again with **half of what's left**.
- Every later turn it warm-starts the search from the current plan for 0.25 seconds, so any drift gets repaired.
- Each turn's drops must fit the 100-unit shed, because overflow is destroyed.

On Kaggle that is about 25 seconds at hour 0 and 13 at hour 1. Gains measured over 57 recorded last days, against the old heuristic:

| search time (desktop)              | coins gained on the last day |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| 0.25 s                             | +275                         |
| 1 s                                | +307                         |
| 2 s                                | +381                         |
| 5 s                                | +434                         |
| 12.7 s (≈ half the bank on Kaggle) | +482                         |

Two-thirds of the gain arrives in the first second or two. One coherent plan for the whole crew is worth more than search time. In one replayed game, last-day harvest went from 103 units to 121. Combined with harvesting melons the day they reach full size, this build beat its predecessor by about 1,250 coins a game.

**2. A shorter route every morning (the last change)** With the last day budgeted, there was still bank to spare from day 13 on. The last build spends about 1.3 seconds on Kaggle each morning improving the dawn plan by large-neighborhood search. It removes a cluster of 2-6 nearby jobs from the routes and reinserts them, plus any dropped jobs nearby, at their cheapest positions. It keeps the change only if the routes come out better: more value covered, or the same value in fewer turns.

I had tried exactly this three days earlier and rejected it: shorter routes, no more coins. What changed was everything around it. By the 30th, idle workers took over jobs they could reach first, so the turns the search freed became real work instead of idle time. It was also kept out of the building phase (days 6-12), where it had cost money. Result: about +700 coins a game against o-v18 in head-to-head play, and +800 on replays against recorded field opponents.

**Which one mattered?** Both agents played the whole post-deadline tournament side by side, and they share the exact last day. The only difference is the morning route search.

|                                          | final rating | vs 1,700-1,900 opponents | vs 2,100+ opponents |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------- |
| Exact last day                           | 1,844        | 53%, +672 a game         | never met one       |
| Exact last day plus morning route search | **2,104**    | 56%, +1,555 a game       | 44% over 158 games  |

Both played about 900 games across the full 14 days, side by side against the same field, so this isn't the early-tournament noise that can separate identical uploads. And against the same band of opponents,  average margin was more than double with morning route search turned on. My read is that the exact last day made the agent solid, and the morning route search made it good enough to hold its own against the 2,000+ field. Both came from noticing that the time bank was sitting unused.

## What I learned about measuring

Most of my time went into this, and it's where I'd start next time.

- **Self-play flatters you.** One build beat its predecessor by 1,300-1,800 coins a game in head-to-head play and was level on the ladder. Both versions farmed the same way, so the test couldn't see what the field would do to it.
- **Replay real games instead.** The test I came to trust restores a recorded ladder game, lets my agent take one seat, and replays the real opponent's moves. Only builds that won both head-to-head (on two separate sets of seeds) and on those replays shipped.
- **Hold the town fixed.** The engine draws one random number per empty tile each night before picking the next shop. So two agents that play differently on the same seed get different towns. My replay test drew new towns for days before I caught it; fixing it cut the noise about five-fold.
- **Judge on margin, not your own coins.** You sell into the same market as your opponent. Several changes raised my coins and lost games, like releasing animals once milk got cheap: the opponent's milk then sold higher. Others cost me coins and won, like the twelfth hand.
- **Watching replays found most of my late gains.** Empty pastures nobody replanted, crops stranded on the last day, a yarn store that opened after the farm was built, and melons left until evening while the opponent sold at hour 7. Each was a concrete defect with a measurable fix.

## What I missed

- **The public notebooks.** I never even clicked on the Code tab until after the deadline. Public agents that finished rated above 2,500 had been up since mid-September, along with careful lab notebooks like Rayk Kretzschmar's. I wouldn't have wanted to fork one: a recorded-script agent built from about 280 numbered patches isn't the kind of building I enjoyed, and I wouldn't have learned the things I did from this competition. But studying them would have shown me where the bar was, and given me strong opponents to test against instead of my own old builds.
- **The fourth quadrant.** On 26 September I watched DSM's best agent run four quadrants, then saw his next two submissions go back to three. I concluded it wasn't worth it. The top agents used it in the end, in the games where it paid: early, for late tomatoes and wool. On a ladder where only your two newest submissions play, a rival's visible behaviour is a signal they control.
- **The opening trick that was being used on me.** On turn 0, buying wheat and selling it straight back raises the price of the opponent's first wheat purchase. Against an opening funded to the coin, that costs a seed. My first opening book kept breaking for "just a few coins" on day 0, and I treated it as bad luck.
- **Trained imitation.** My attempt 3 imitated only the opening, and the opening went stale. The top teams cloned the whole policy from replays of the best players and kept retargeting the newest versions, and at least two reached the top 10 training on a single desktop GPU. I spent many, many hours on labor routing and efficiency in particular, and some of the top teams completely sidestepped that issue with a trained model that learned to be more efficient than my agent was without needing to understand why.

- **HowardLeeTW**, whose opening I studied and tested early on.

Happy to answer questions about any of it.

When deploying small edge models for regional or code-mixed languages, how do you enforce strict semantic grounding to prevent linguistic drift and unverified hallucination inside agent loops?

text:
First, I'd like to thank my teammates, **tetsuya** and **guoqin gu**. It was a pleasure taking part in this competition together. Thanks also to the hosts and everyone who shared strategies and experiences in the discussions.

# Overview

Our final agent is an **18.4M-parameter Transformer + CNN policy** trained by behavior cloning on strong game replays. It directly predicts worker commands and market orders, using EMA weights and single-model argmax decoding.

| Final agent | At a glance |
| --- | --- |
| Policy | 18.4M parameters · Transformer + farm CNN |
| Learning | Behavior cloning · EMA weights |
| Final replay mixture | 70% MMPQ · 30% other sources |
| Inference | Single model · FP32 · argmax · CPU AOT |

Development began with RL and later shifted toward BC as the replay pipeline and model improved. The sections below describe the training setup, the development timeline and the final agent.

# Training pipeline

The final submission uses behavior cloning with normalized replay targets, weighted source sampling and auxiliary objectives. A later PPO branch starts from a BC actor and continues training through interaction with opponents.

*Figure 1. The final BC submission pipeline and our later direct-action PPO branch. Our early RL exploration preceded this final setup.*

Three design choices were central to the final agent:

- **Requested actions and executed actions can differ.** We reconstructed execution effects before building BC targets.

- **Decisions within a turn depend on one another.** Workers and market orders are decoded in execution order, with later decisions seeing the resource changes caused by earlier ones.

- **A single observation does not describe the market process.** We added history statistics at multiple timescales, together with economic and forecasting objectives.

## Behavior cloning: replay data and action labels

Competition replays are converted into player-side trajectories containing observations, history and actions. The final fine-tuning corpus contains 4,996 trajectories from 38 submissions, or approximately 3.59 million action time steps.

**Replay requests can differ from executed actions.** A worker may request more items than remain available, a market order may receive no fill, or a command may have no effect. Cloning these requests directly can leave the action targets inconsistent with subsequent state changes.

Our preprocessing reconstructs execution: ineffective worker commands become PASS, quantities are corrected, unfilled market orders become NOOP, and sales can use SELL ALL. BC imitates this normalized command sequence.

## Mixing replay sources

BC starts with pretraining on high-scoring replays, followed by adjustments to replay sources and sampling weights. The final branch continues from an earlier BC checkpoint with a 70:30 mixture of MMPQ and other replays.

The corpus contains 1,165 MMPQ trajectories and 3,831 from other sources. The 70% sampling share deliberately emphasizes a relatively consistent group of strategies while retaining behavior from other sources.

## Training objectives

Action imitation is combined with economic and forecasting objectives. Economic targets cover labor, land, cash, cash margin, stock and field service. Forecast targets describe subsequent market and economic changes in the replay, giving the shared encoder supervision beyond the next action.

The total loss is:

```text
L = 2 * worker NLL + market NLL
    + economic loss + 0.05 * forecast loss
```

Future replay frames are used to construct targets only. During play, the policy consumes current legal observations and the history maintained so far.

Compressed trajectory pools and rotating sampling keep random reads and memory use manageable.

## Reinforcement learning: BC initialization and PPO

The later direct-action RL implementation initializes the actor from BC and uses PPO to continue learning against a mixture of opponents. This branch is distinct from the early RL experiments that motivated the initial approach.

A vectorized JAX simulator collects on-policy data, with 512 games per rollout wave across four GPUs. Early experiments mainly used self-play. The later opponent mixture has five approximately equal groups: self-play and four groups of frozen neural opponents.

The later reward emphasizes terminal win/loss and adds a cash-margin signal. With margin m and s(m)=tanh(m/100000):

```text
r = 0.25 * (s(m_next) - s(m_now))
    + terminal * (sign(m_next) + 0.25 * s(m_next))
```

PPO uses gamma 0.995, GAE lambda 0.95, ratio clipping to [0.8, 1.2] and normalized advantages. The actor learning rate is 1e-6; the independent critic uses 3e-4. Policy sampling and PPO likelihood evaluation both use temperature 0.5.

Two parts received particular attention. The first was **critic initialization**: after changing the reward, we held the actor fixed and fitted returns from complete games, holding out whole games for validation. The second was **controlling policy movement**: after each proposed update, we checked KL on both the update minibatch and a fixed reference minibatch from that rollout, reverting proposals that exceeded the limits.

# Training history

*Figure 2. Four milestones in our competition. The final BC model came from a continuation run in the last two or three hours.*

## RL exploration and scaling

Early experiments established that RL was viable in this environment. Once the training pipeline was working, further development focused on improving the policy and scaling training.

*Learning through trial and error. A conceptual illustration of our early RL exploration.*

Scaling produced substantial improvements, but issues in the JAX implementation and model design slowed iteration. Limited experience with these parts of the system contributed to longer debugging cycles and made scaling less effective than expected.

## Shift toward BC

Strong BC agents from other teams prompted a renewed focus on imitation learning during the final week. The last three days of development concentrated on correcting weaknesses in the BC training pipeline, followed by changes to the policy model.

In local testing, the revised BC models substantially outperformed the RL models available at that stage. Further RL training was also tested, but improvements arrived more slowly, so the remaining development focused on BC.

A further BC continuation ran during the final two or three hours before the deadline. Local testing identified its step197129 EMA checkpoint as the strongest candidate available at that point, and it was selected for submission.

*Learning from replays, with one last experiment near the deadline. A conceptual illustration of the final BC run.*

# Architecture and inference

*Figure 3. Main policy pathways. History and spatial features condition the entity representation; the resource ledger connects worker and market decoding.*

## Entity Transformer and farm CNN

The state is represented as entity tokens: a global state, workers, tiles, shops, commodities and project features. Attention connects these entities, including relationships between workers and tiles, production and inventory, and the player's farm and the shared market.

The backbone has two interaction rounds. Each round processes worker and field tokens in separate branches before shared attention exchanges information. A residual 5×5 CNN additionally processes our own 10×10 farm. The opponent's public farm participates through entity features.

| Component | Final configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Parameters | 18,425,190 |
| Transformer width | 288 |
| Feed-forward width | 224 |
| Attention heads | 4 |
| Entity-branch and shared-attention rounds | 2 |
| Own-farm CNN | Two 5×5 convolutions, 63→224→960 channels, projected to width 288 |

History is represented by rolling means and lagged differences, with windows of 6, 24, 72, 168, 360 and 719 turns. These statistics can be updated incrementally during play and cached during preprocessing, allowing BC to sample random time steps without unrolling an entire game.

## Sequential action decoding

Worker actions are factorized into direction, local operation, argument and quantity. During autonomous play, commands are generated in worker execution order, updating the resource ledger after each one. Items taken by an earlier worker therefore change the inventory context available to the next worker.

*Earlier actions change what remains available. A conceptual illustration of the resource ledger used in sequential decoding.*

During BC training, causal prefixes are precomputed from demonstrated actions. Worker losses can then be evaluated in parallel while preserving within-turn dependencies.

The market decoder similarly generates up to ten ordered slots, conditioning each one on the prefix updated by earlier orders. Quantities support numeric values and SELL ALL. The final policy emits commands directly, without an additional state-dependent legality mask.

## CPU deployment

Inference uses one model, FP32 weights and conditional-head argmax. To fit the competition's CPU runtime, we compiled the initial forward pass, subsequent forward pass and history update ahead of time for Broadwell CPUs.

We also fixed persistent inventory insertion order in the deployment adapter. This affects which items survive DROP when shed capacity is insufficient, and therefore changes later states. We maintain the order from consecutive observations so deployment follows the execution semantics used in training. The final package passed a complete-season raw-source execution check.

# Evaluation and checkpoint selection

Local evaluation uses fixed historical BC agents as opponents. Each comparison contains 512 seeds, with both seats played on every seed, for 1,024 games per pairing. Deterministic argmax matches submission-time decoding.

The final step197129 EMA achieved the following results. Draws are not counted as wins, and cash margin is our terminal cash minus the opponent's.

*Figure 4. Strict win rates and mean terminal cash margins against five historical BC opponents. Each pairing contains 1,024 games with both seats on every seed.*

| Opponent | W / L / D | Win rate | Mean cash margin |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Earlier BC 0.40 | 944 / 80 / 0 | 92.19% | +4,935 |
| Split2 BC 0.45 | 900 / 124 / 0 | 87.89% | +3,770 |
| Double BC 0.25 | 876 / 148 / 0 | 85.55% | +3,623 |
| Stage14 BC 0.25 | 861 / 163 / 0 | 84.08% | +3,338 |
| 37.3M BC step41000 | 781 / 243 / 0 | 76.27% | +2,301 |

These results are from our local JAX simulator against the fixed historical panel used for checkpoint comparison.

## Final checkpoint selection

Our final checkpoint is the stage 3 EMA at step197129, saved when the mean of the last twenty raw-model total training losses reached approximately 0.50. Training later continued to step202752, but the later checkpoint did not improve every matchup. Across four common opponents, the two checkpoints won 3,581 and 3,579 games respectively, with different strengths by opponent.

Checkpoint selection considered complete-game performance alongside BC loss. The loss measures fit to demonstrations; local matches test behavior over a full season. These comparisons do not isolate the effects of model size, training data or optimization.

Submission remained uncertain: a comparable model had not yet been tested on the leaderboard, and an earlier submission had failed to generalize due to overfitting. This checkpoint was submitted once and became the team's highest-scoring submission.

# Discussion and future work

**Iteration speed.** Scaling improved the models, but implementation and architecture issues limited experiment throughput. Faster validation and more reliable training code would have made successive changes easier to assess.

**Data quality starts with execution semantics.** In a sequential environment, action names and requested quantities do not fully describe a sample. Within-turn resource changes, partial fills and ineffective commands all belong in the data pipeline.

**Replay distribution and the BC-to-RL transition.** Further work would compare teacher consistency, behavioral diversity and sampling weights, then examine critic pretraining, opponent selection and policy-update stability under matched training and evaluation conditions.

# Acknowledgements

Thanks again to **tetsuya** and **guoqin gu** for sharing this competition journey. Thanks to the hosts for the environment and replay access, and to the competitors who shared strategies, code and discussions. Strong replays provided the foundation for our final BC agent, and the community's work helped us throughout the competition.

text:
Thanks to Kaggle for another fun Playground episode. Team A.Ş finished **17th of 3,575** on the private leaderboard (**0.94571**). The whole pipeline of our own three models is in a public notebook that runs end-to-end on a Kaggle T4 in 3.3 hours: **[17th Place Solution – Playground S6E9](https://www.kaggle.com/code/ahmetbugrahanaltunok/17th-place-solution-playground-s6e9)**.

Convention: 1u = 1e-5 ROC AUC.

## TL;DR

- **The recipe is the floor, the generator is the signal.** `1.2·income/100k + 0.6·concern + 2·subsidy − anxiety > 5.5` alone scores 0.9377. Everything above it came from artifacts of how the rows were generated: income behaves like a ~14.7k-level category, and numbers are written as GPT-2 BPE tokens.
- **Three own models, one blend.** A core XGBoost with fold-safe target encodings (sliding windows, anchors, hierarchical shrinkage ladders over income and GPT-2 token prefixes), a generator-aware ridge logistic regression, and an LR → XGBoost stack. Weighted logit-rank average: **OOF 0.94667**.
- **Decisions on OOF, not on the public board.** With 669k OOF rows a paired comparison is ~3.4× more precise than on the 57k public rows. Every accepted change had to hold on 20/20 random half-splits of the OOF.
- **What moved private was changing what the models see.** From 19 to 30 September private went 0.94548 → 0.94571 (+23u). Adding other people's *predictions* to the blend moved it ~0–2u; new models and features (the generator-aware LR basis and our extensions to it, GPT-2 token ladders, the stack) moved it ~21u.

## 1. The data and the generator

- **Recipe.** [Chris Deotte's EDA](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/playground-series-s6e9/discussion/739303) recovered the purchase rule. Fitting the five coefficients on the 669k rows ourselves gave nearly the same numbers (except High anxiety, which only ~2k rows determine) and only +8u over the untrained formula.
- **Income is a category.** ~98% of rows carry an income value that also appears in the original 10k data; the median value is shared by ~200 rows. Each value carries its own small bias, so *target statistics per value* are the main lever — but they are noisy, so how you shrink them matters more than which model reads them.
- **Numbers are tokens.** The generator emits `" 87431"` as `" 8" | "74" | "31"`. Incomes that share a token prefix share a hidden bias, so the token prefix is a better "parent" for shrinkage than a decimal bucket.
- **Four deterministic regions** are pure in train and pushed to the ends at the very last step: income ≥ 170,537 → all buy; 31,004–41,970 → nobody; commute ≥ 83 km → nobody; income at the 30k floor with no subsidy and (concern = 1 or anxiety ≠ Low) → nobody.

## 2. Validation

- `StratifiedKFold(20, shuffle=True, random_state=42)`, **the same split for all three models**, so OOFs can be blended and compared row by row.
- Every label-derived feature is **cross-fitted inside the fold**: validation and test rows use the whole fold-train, fold-train rows use an inner 5-fold. Leave-one-out encoding cost −670u — trees read the row's own label back from it.
- A gain was accepted only if it was positive on **20/20 random half-splits** of the OOF (choose on half A, score on half B).
- For reading the public board I used the paired standard error between two of my own files, `SE ≈ 0.0020·√(1−ρ)` (ρ = Spearman between the files). At our typical ρ ≈ 0.999 that is ~6u — the size of most single steps — so the public LB served only as a sanity check.

## 3. Models

| member | what it is | OOF AUC | ρ with core | weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core XGBoost | recipe + multi-resolution features + fold-safe encodings, 2 rounds | 0.946502 | 1 | 1.0 |
| Generator-aware LR | ~425 cross-fitted log-odds features, ridge, L-BFGS | 0.946527 | 0.990 | 0.8 |
| LR → XGB stack | same basis + out-of-fold LR logit → shallow XGBoost | 0.946480 | 0.975 | 0.4 |
| **Blend** (logit-rank) | | **0.946672** | | |

*(OOF numbers from the public notebook's 20-fold run; the core is round 1, which is the honest one.)*

**Core XGBoost.** Features: the recipe score and its margin to 5.5, recipe interactions, 30k/5 km floor flags, income and commute digits, train+test value frequencies, income // 100…5000, commute // 0.5…5, modulo remainders, and a per-fold logistic "linear base". Inside each fold:

- sklearn `TargetEncoder` on 29 keys (raw columns, digits, income floored at 1/10/100/1k/10k, commute at 0.1/1/10) at three smoothings;
- **window encoders** — target rate of incomes within ±2…±500 $, on non-decimal buckets (//25, //250, //2500), and on the nearest "anchor" income (a value seen ≥ 10 times). Bucket edges are arbitrary; windows and anchors put them elsewhere;
- **hierarchical ladders** — one column that shrinks the income rate coarse → fine (10k → 1k → 100 → 10 → 1), each level towards the previous one; the same for commute and for **GPT-2 token prefix → two-token prefix → exact value**.

`max_bin=4096` (the label is a sharp threshold on a continuous score; 256 bins blur it, +128u when found), `colsample_bytree=0.10`, `max_depth=4`, `lr=0.01`. Round 2 retrains with the round-1 test predictions added to every encoder as soft labels; its OOF is leaky, so only its test prediction is used.

**Generator-aware LR.** Built on [Paul Bryan Elefante's public notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/heuljax/kps6e09-generator-aware-ridge-logistic-regression) (token × context cells, token-prefix chains, composition features). Our additions: **k-means clusters of the GPT-2 embedding vectors** of the income tokens (so similar-looking tokens share strength), commute tokens, and **auxiliary non-target features** — a LightGBM predicts each input column from the others, and its prediction, residual and |residual| tell how "typical" the row is for the generator. Its value was not its solo score but its decorrelation: ρ = 0.990 with the core is the most decorrelated *strong* member we ever found.

**Stack.** The LR basis plus the LR logit (out-of-fold even for fold-train rows, via an inner 5-fold) into an XGBoost with `max_depth=5`. The trees fix what the linear model's additivity gets wrong.

## 4. Blend

Weighted average of `logit(rank)` with weights 1.0 / 0.8 / 0.4, then the four rules. Ranks remove the scale differences between members; the logit keeps the tails apart. The weight surface is a plateau (0.946665–0.946673 over lr 0.6–1.0 × stack 0.2–0.6), so we never tuned it further.

The submitted file also contained public notebooks' predictions (Paul's XGB, RealMLP, LightGBM/XGB models by other authors, a bagged ± selection over ~30 public OOFs) — together roughly +1u OOF on top of the three models above — and a small public-LB-tuned correction that the OOF disliked. The notebook leaves both out.

## 5. How the score moved

Every honest step from 19 to 30 September, public and private:

| file | change | public | private |
|---|---|---|---|
| 072 | own XGBoost core + 3 public-notebook slots | 0.94655 | 0.94548 |
| 083 | + Paul's XGB | 0.94655 | 0.94550 |
| 092 | + 4 more public notebooks | 0.94656 | 0.94550 |
| 095 | 40-fold core + Paul's generator-aware LR | 0.94673 | 0.94562 |
| 097 | LR with GPT-2 embedding clusters + commute tokens | 0.94677 | 0.94563 |
| 101 | core with GPT-2 token ladders | 0.94676 | 0.94565 |
| 103 | + LR → XGB stack | 0.94677 | 0.94566 |
| 108 | LR with auxiliary non-target features | 0.94679 | 0.94568 |
| **117** | stack variants averaged (final pick) | **0.94689** | **0.94571** |

Public and private moved together at almost every step that changed what a model sees; other people's predictions added to the blend barely moved either.

**Final selection:** 117 (0.94571) and 108 (0.94568), both honest blends. Our best *public* score on the leaderboard (0.94704) was an unselected public-LB experiment built on the same blend; its private is the same 0.94571 as its honest base, so it neither helped nor hurt.

## 6. What did not work

| idea | effect |
|---|---|
| Several fold partitions / seed averaging of the same model | test predictions correlate 0.9999; public identical |
| Learned stackers (LR / LightGBM on members' ranks, ± raw features) | −17u (shallow GBDT) to −250u (with raw features); more flexible = worse |
| Negative weights for weak members | knife-edge: +0.4u at −0.05, −1.4u at −0.10 |
| Decorrelated but weaker members (own RealMLP ρ 0.979, gated cross-net) | 0 / −1u; a member must be within ~20u of the best single model |
| Original 10k rows as training rows | −2.7u at weight 1, −68u at weight 10 |
| Original-data target means per value; the "parent" row a row was copied from | +0.8u; parent recipe AUC 0.56 vs 0.94 |
| Monotone constraints in XGBoost | −7u |
| Triple-interaction target encoding | 286 combinations, none positive |
| Near-duplicate label injection (12 of 13 columns match) | negative at every weight |
| Pseudo-labels inside the LR's encoders | public unchanged |

## Code

**[17th Place Solution – Playground S6E9](https://www.kaggle.com/code/ahmetbugrahanaltunok/17th-place-solution-playground-s6e9)** — EDA, features, the three models and the blend in one notebook (GPU + Internet, 3.3 h on a T4; `QUICK_RUN = True` checks the pipeline in a few minutes). The core's code reproduces our final core exactly (checked bit-for-bit on a subsample); the notebook uses 20 folds instead of 40 to fit the time limit.

## Acknowledgements

- **Chris Deotte** — the EDA that recovered the recipe.
- **Paul Bryan Elefante** — the generator-aware ridge logistic regression and the XGB_SAMPLE notebook.
- **Omkar Kadam** — the original dataset.
- My teammate **settdata**.

**Tools:** AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Codex) helped write code and run analyses; every number above comes from our own runs.

Congratulations to Chris Deotte, Team Alicia, M & M, Prior and everyone who took part — see you in the next episode!

I evaluated OpenAI’s open Whisper models (`tiny`, `base`, `small`) running locally via faster-whisper on CPU using self-recorded Urdu-English code-switched clinical consultations[cite: 15].

* **Error Rate Scaling:** Scaling from `tiny` to `small` cut the Word Error Rate (WER) from 43.8% down to 19.2%[cite: 15].
* **The Clinical Term Recall Gap:** Despite lower overall WER, clinical key-term recall stagnated between 50% and 54%[cite: 15]. Critical medical code-switched terms (like *X-ray*, *MRI*, *Physiotherapy*) consistently failed or were phonetically corrupted[cite: 17].
* **Orthographic vs. Semantic Integrity:** While the Character Error Rate dropped to 7.7% (indicating minor spelling variations like dropped aspirated letters), downstream automated parsing or red-flag regex extractors fail on such corrupted tokens[cite: 16, 17].

What strategies (such as domain-specific prompt prefixing or vocabulary biasing without full fine-tuning) have proven most effective for handling code-switched medical terminology in Whisper?

text:
**28th place · Gold · Kaggriculture 2026**
*A learned policy controls the first ten days; a planner then chooses what to grow, who does the work, and when to sell.* **Team 吃白饭的大肥鱼** — Gengsr · 醇久 (deepios) · TanPowasd · Tang Di24 [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F130a3b62a9279f9fad630c9ab3b916c6%2F01_three_stage_system.png?generation=1792200935819421&alt=media) **Illustration 01 · From the opening policy to the planner** *Read from left to right: opening actions, the handover of recorded history, and continued planning. From day 10, daily plans coordinate future production, labor and purchases, while the hourly executor compares the next actions using new observations. The bottom strip marks the transition and main settings.* A farm can look profitable and still run out of cash before its next harvest. Crops need care, animals need feed, and workers must deliver goods to the shed before they can be sold. Our Kaggriculture agent had to choose what to produce while keeping that whole sequence affordable and executable, hour by hour, until the season ended. Games involving Majkel1337, DSM, M & M & P & Q and DECEM showed several ways to manage these dependencies. A small cash balance could be enough when a delivery was about to fund the next purchase. A much larger balance could hide a farm with too little production capacity. We built the agent around the work and income still ahead: when each crop would mature, who could service it, when goods would reach the shed, and what both farms might earn from the shared market. We finished **28th of 10,148 teams**, with a **gold medal** and a final leaderboard score of **5111.2**. Our highest-scoring submission was **56720575**, the re-submitted **C2O7** agent. That leaderboard score is a competition rating, distinct from the cash earned inside an individual game. [Official final standings](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/leaderboard) Our agent used a learned policy for the first ten days, followed by a Rust planner for the rest of the game. The opening network coordinated setup actions. The planner chose production projects, assigned workers, built routes and scheduled sales within a limited computation budget. We also submitted a later experimental branch in our other final slot. We discuss its experiments separately from C2O7, because several late changes improved local measurements while the earlier agent produced our best final leaderboard result. This article follows the decisions the agent had to make: learn a coordinated opening, plan production and labor at dawn, then revise routes, purchases and sales as each hour unfolds. The experiments show where that design worked and where an apparently useful improvement failed to help the complete agent. During the final week, we used a Chinese-made PPU accelerator platform for learning alongside CPU simulation and game evaluation. ## 1. Turn production into cash before the season ends Each player operates a separate 10×10 farm, starting with one unlocked quadrant and the option to buy more land. Crops and animals take inputs, work and time to produce goods. Workers move between tiles, carry items and perform jobs; the farm sells its output into shared product markets whose prices respond to inventory. The configured season lasts 30 days, and the final reward is the player's money. Assets therefore help only through income that the farm can earn and settle before termination. [Official game documentation](https://github.com/Kaggle/kaggle-environments/blob/28b6d8af3ce73926b3d0fda1410c1ddd8384ab8c/kaggle_environments/envs/kaggriculture/README.md), [interpreter](https://github.com/Kaggle/kaggle-environments/blob/28b6d8af3ce73926b3d0fda1410c1ddd8384ab8c/kaggle_environments/envs/kaggriculture/kaggriculture.py) ### The same cash balance can hide different farms [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F012c20ee2310fba9e83534b08a6223d9%2F02_equal_cash_different_farms.png?generation=1792201031229941&alt=media) **Illustration 02 · Equal cash, different farms** *The schematic farms differ in crop ages, unfinished work and goods in transit. Dotted connections link current resources to possible future sales, showing which future receipts a farm valuation needs to consider.* One historical game showed how little a cash balance reveals about future production. At the beginning of day 16, our cash balance was **31,771** and DECEM's was **31,710**. Six days earlier, DECEM had sold a batch of melons and bought its fourth land quadrant in the same hour. We sold our melons too; by the following hour we had **7,712** in cash, but stayed at three quadrants. The almost equal cash balances on day 16 belonged to different farms: DECEM had more land, more tomatoes and more strawberries, with work still needed to turn those assets into money. We finished that game with **80,713 to DECEM's 99,340**. The cash gap narrowed by 2,344 on the last day, so most of it had accumulated before final liquidation. This was **CAND2 against DECEM**, episode **115509423**: CAND2 used the same native planner as C2O7 but an earlier opening checkpoint. The two farms reached almost equal cash balances with different production capacity and different work still ahead. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F13ec4980699c4c50aac9fb1d5b23d324%2FA_cash_and_capacity.png?generation=1792201097719483&alt=media) *Data figure A. Cash at the start of each day and at termination in episode 115509423. The lower panel shows unlocked quadrants. At day 16, CAND2 and DECEM had almost equal cash balances and different land and production capacity.* ### Connect each production choice to the work and sale it requires “Grow more tomatoes” therefore leaves most of the work undecided. The planner must find a tile that will be available in time, pay for seed without interrupting feed purchases, assign someone to plant and water it, and return for later care. It must check when the first harvest arrives and whether the remaining harvests can justify the setup before the season ends. It must also find workers who can collect the output and reach the shed before the intended sale. When several projects mature together, those projects compete for the same labor and storage. A forecast price alone cannot settle these choices. A crop may look profitable but consume a worker needed elsewhere. An affordable worker may have no useful task that can be reached in time. An expansion may promise a positive return but miss the hour when cash, inputs and labor are all available. We needed the planner to represent each part of the proposed sequence so that a failed plan could be traced to the missing money, work, delivery or sale. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F0f27398abbd1b5520d70b7b0b70fd84b%2F03_seed_to_cash.png?generation=1792201125033971&alt=media) **Illustration 03 · The work behind a sale** *Inputs and care produce goods; workers harvest, carry and deliver them; market orders turn the stock into cash. Following this sequence connects a production schedule to the next purchase it can finance.* Majkel1337 showed why delivery belonged inside the investment calculation. In episode **110620339**, its farmer carried six units of wool at day 6, hour 3, while cash was only **303**. Dropping the wool put it in the shed, but the land order still failed. Selling those six units in the following hour raised cash to **1,588**. At hour 5, the farm bought its second quadrant and three units of wheat, leaving **495**. Majkel submission **56216119** was playing THIRD FARM CLUB **56326604**. The wool already had value in the farmer's bag, but it could pay for land only after delivery and sale. Both farms can produce the same good, so neither can value a harvest in isolation. A large batch may begin selling at a high price and end at a much lower one. Above the price floor, our own output changes market inventory as it is sold; the rival's output can reach the market while ours is still growing. The value of a crop therefore depends on the production and sales calendars of both farms. Data figure B shows this price response for six products, using the official rule when inventory is above its reference level. All panels use the same horizontal scale. Wheat and eggs decline slowly over the plotted range, while strawberry, milk and wool prices reach the floor with comparatively little surplus. Melon follows a different nonlinear curve. These differences make the timing and combination of production important: each product encounters a different price response as the farms sell their output. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F5a237c6cd806adcce07eca0b44e5d653%2FB_market_curves.png?generation=1792201154742054&alt=media) *Data figure B. Instantaneous price quotes from the official `MARKET_PARAMS` and `market_price` function, including integer rounding and the floor. Each panel has its own price scale; surplus inventory units share one horizontal scale. A batch settles unit by unit along the changing quotes. At the price floor, a sale credits cash while market inventory stays unchanged.* The market connects the players through prices. When we sell, the interpreter credits our account. Our rule required no observed regression in mean margin, so the package failed that gate despite winning two more games. Both the wins and the smaller margin can be explained by the recorded scores. Our final score rose by **123.2** on average, while Rall's score in those separate games rose by **607.8**, giving a margin change of **−484.5**. Forty-five pairs improved and fifty-one worsened. The two baseline losses converted into wins contributed **+13,603** points of total margin change; the remaining 94 pairs contributed **−60,119**. A comfortable win that becomes a smaller win still counts as one win. All of these quantities use the game scores returned by the Rall evaluation. The tape screen and Rall test use different opponent populations and protocols, including whether the rival responds to our actions. We treated them as separate stages of evaluation. The proposal that had reduced idle hours in behavior checks went on to win more Rall games with a smaller average advantage. Final margin captured a change that the job and win counts missed. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2Fba145bf004f7f9406483eb9cfb6db59f%2FD_protocol_change.png?generation=1792201417272145&alt=media) *Data figure D. The same frozen package produces +426.0 in 320 tape cells and −484.5 in 96 paired reactive Rall cells. Error bars show ±1 episode-cluster SE for the tape screen and ±1 seed-cluster SE for Rall. The two tests use separate opponent populations and timing protocols.* ### A better codebook changed nothing because the chosen branch did not read it In another final-night experiment, we refitted a 1,024-entry trajectory codebook without changing its deployed hyperparameters. The codebook compresses similar historical situations and the distributions of net flows over the next four hours. Its held-out forecast tests improved, including the required short-horizon CRPS measures. But the package still selected `mk_flow=1`, which used Blend. Only the alternative `mk_flow=2/3` branches consumed the refreshed codebook. With that configuration unchanged, the new package and its predecessor had identical score margins and win outcomes in every one of the **320 cells**. The refreshed resource performed better when evaluated directly, but the active decision path never read it. This failure was a useful reminder to connect a model experiment to the configuration and code that actually consume its output. ### Choose an opening the later planner can continue Opening selection brought the same issue into the first ten days. In a 97-cell comparison with the same later controller, openings from our own lineage produced positive mean changes, while two openings cloned from strong opponents produced negative ones. An older own-lineage checkpoint also retained more of the baseline's already-winning games than the newer checkpoint. A strong opening had to leave a farm our particular controller could use: crop ages, worker locations, upcoming deliveries and maintenance obligations all mattered alongside cash. One earlier handover experiment made that dependency especially clear. A cold-started planner cleared **eleven strawberry plots that were still producing**, replacing work the opening had already invested in. We added a short protection period for crops already productive at takeover. Moving the handover earlier also changed where it fell in the opening's cash cycle: the planner could inherit the costs before the corresponding harvest receipts arrived. These experiences made continuity part of the design. The incoming controller needed to preserve useful commitments, service the inherited farm and carry its financing sequence forward. ### Train models on PPU accelerators and test agents on CPU workers We increased accelerator capacity gradually during the final week, reaching **four ZW810-family cards** later in the week. The PPU-ZW810E platform provided a **48-core CPU quota and 336 GiB of system memory**. Learning jobs produced model resources for the agent, while CPU Slurm workers handled simulation and game evaluation. These were different workloads even when they ran on infrastructure that also contained accelerators. The opponent-network training script used the `cuda:0` software interface and trained for 12 epochs. The underlying hardware was a Chinese-made PPU platform. Alibaba Cloud documents the PPU-ZW810 family, while T-Head's SAIL documentation names PPU-ZW810E / Zhenwu 810E. [PPU-SMI documentation](https://help.aliyun.com/en/document_detail/2971881.html), [T-Head documentation](https://github.com/t-head/vllm-sail/blob/cc1b67eaa1bee9a7f375baaef16dff4015650fd1/docs/user_guide/supported_features.md) A learning update still had to pass through the CPU agent before it could affect a game. We exported the model resource, combined it with the intended code and configuration, compiled the agent, and evaluated that executable. Build scripts staged an explicit source-file list, locked source snapshots and compiled in node-local temporary directories. Separate target directories and cached build products reduced repeated compilation. We recorded content hashes for the source and executable together with the configuration, toolchain, runner and evaluation protocol, so results stayed associated with the version that produced them. That separation also helped diagnose failures across machines. One data refresh encountered a Cargo cache collision in the tooling build and a Python ABI mismatch when importing evaluation code. Those failures called for repairs to the build or evaluation environment, rather than changes to the candidate policy. Keeping model fitting, packaging and game evaluation as separate stages let us rerun the failed stage with the intended inputs. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2Fa760eead444a2b22b95dbb253c846078%2F15_compute_workflow.png?generation=1792201429261770&alt=media) **Illustration 15 · From training a model to running games** *Learning jobs train and export models on PPUs, the build combines code, weights and configuration, and CPU workers run games. Version identifiers carry through these steps so each test result maps to the program that produced it.* ## 5. C2O7 was the submission selected by the final leaderboard We kept two submissions for the final evaluation: C2O7 and a later experimental branch. C2O7 combined the established native planner with the OV7 v90 opening, while the other package carried further changes from the final development period. CAND2 and C2O7 used the same native planner and configuration. The change between them was the opening checkpoint, from OV2 v293 to OV7 v90. We first submitted C2O7 as **56687882**, then submitted it again as **56720575** in the final pair. The other slot, **56720565**, contained **cx_blr_o7_r20** with later changes. The final leaderboard identifies the re-submitted C2O7 as our highest-scoring agent. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2Fb39f79a84739ed778182d613361dd47b%2F16_version_and_evidence.png?generation=1792201443308704&alt=media) **Illustration 16 · The two final submissions** *The upper lane follows the re-submitted C2O7, whose result appears on the final leaderboard. The lower lane follows the later experimental agent into the other final slot. Code, opening weights and configuration together identify each agent.* The earlier agent that we retained produced our best final result. Several changes from the last night improved their target measurements without replacing it as the stronger submission. Those experiments were still informative: they showed how better prediction could stop short of different decisions, and how different decisions could stop short of a larger advantage. Keeping C2O7 in the final pair let both versions compete in the final evaluation. ## 6. Make the chosen investment survive through execution Our clearest direction for improvement is to keep more of the proposed investment together throughout planning. Buying land has value only with a continuation: which tiles will be used, what must be bought, who will do the first useful work, and which later receipts will repay the expense. A promising continuation can lose that value if a later stage changes the work or sale schedule on which it depended. The fourth-quadrant purchase logic operates within a **day 10–12** window. Our CAND2 game against DECEM drew attention to what must happen within that window: once cash becomes available, the new land needs a useful production plan and workers who can carry it out. The land-purchase logic shows a concrete place to improve this consistency. It first creates a trial farm with the new quadrant and optimizes projects on the new tiles. For the purchase decision, it then creates **two additional copies**: one without the purchase and one with it. Both copies are reoptimized across **all tiles**, using the same post-purchase sweep budget. The estimated gain is the value of the reoptimized farm with land, minus the reoptimized farm without it, minus the purchase price. Thus both sides of the comparison can rearrange existing production. The comparison copies are used to make the purchase decision. When the dawn path adopts the purchase directly, it installs the earlier trial that initially optimized only the new tiles, then runs the usual subsequent optimization across the farm. The implementation therefore distinguishes the plan used to justify buying from the plan that starts the next optimization. Preserving a profitable continuation more directly through that transition is a useful development target, along with keeping its cash commitments and worker routes consistent. Land can also be bought during the day. A qualifying dawn verdict can enable an intraday capital proposal once cash is available. That proposal can generate new economic projects with the crop dynamic program, simulate the purchase and evaluate the work that follows. A separate purchase-only branch can acquire land for the next morning when the search finds no worthwhile plan for using it today. This gives the agent several ways to expand, with different timing and funding conditions. Keeping these paths consistent would let the agent compare the timing and financing of expansion more directly. Candidate generation is another place where a specific change may matter more than a better forecast. The main configuration filters out **new strawberry-planting candidates after day 15**, while leaving existing strawberries in place. A forecast cannot favor a planting that never reaches the evaluator. We would revisit such filters together with maturity dates, remaining harvests, labor and terminal sale opportunities, so the planner can compare complete late-season uses of a tile. The daily and hourly calculations should also agree more closely about how output becomes income. A daily production project can look attractive under one assumed sale schedule while its actual route requires another. More workers help only when they can reach useful jobs and deliver goods in time. Improving that connection means comparing project choices using the routes and sale opportunities the farm can actually execute, then retaining the chosen continuation as later decisions revise it. The experiments suggest different tests for each improvement. For a new opponent model, examine whether it changes the selected feasible plan and whether that change helps. For extra work or a different crew, measure the final margin as well as completed jobs and win count. For a refreshed resource, verify that the active decision path uses it. W17, the late-hours package and the unused codebook produced different outcomes at these stages, pointing to different changes in the system. The strongest opponents made these dependencies visible in ordinary actions. Majkel delivered and sold wool before expanding. M&M used an ordered sale and purchase sequence to turn milk into a sheep and land within one hour. DSM funded immediate obligations while holding other goods for later. Our agent combined learned opening decisions with explicit planning to manage the same kinds of commitments. Our next priority is to carry a valuable sequence of work, purchases and sales all the way from proposal to execution. ## Acknowledgments We thank Kaggle and the environment authors for a game with rules we could study precisely. - The 12B solved less than half as many tasks as the 31B in every setting I tried.

**Limits:** 31 tasks from four repositories, one or two runs per setting, timing on an A100 rather than the scorer's four L4 GPUs. Differences of one or two tasks would be noise here; the gap between 31B and 12B was the same in both runs.

Per-task results are in [Gemma 4 Task Soundness and Local Results](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dmitriigluzdov/gemma-4-task-soundness-and-local-results); speed measurements are in [Gemma 4 Serving and LoRA Verification Kit](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dmitriigluzdov/gemma-4-serving-and-lora-verification-kit). # Q-FT: a Qwen transformer that reads tabular rows as embeddings

Kaggle Playground S6E10 (airline satisfaction, ROC AUC). How each row of the table is turned into vectors, fed into
Qwen3-0.6B, and trained; what LoRA does; and what we found.

**At a glance**
- **0.959795**: 5-fold OOF AUC, raw features only.
- **22**: positions per row (21 feature tokens + 1 CLS).
- **10.1M**: trainable LoRA parameters on a frozen 0.6B backbone.
- **~52 min**: per fold on one A100 (3 epochs, ~920 rows/s).

## 1. The idea in one picture

A language model normally reads *tokens* such as words. Q-FT skips text entirely:
1. It converts each **feature** of a row into one learned vector the same size as Qwen's word vectors (1,024 numbers).
2. It hands those vectors straight to Qwen.
3. It reads the answer from the last position.

It's the same trick vision-language models use for image patches.

## 2. How one feature becomes one token

Every one of the 21 columns gets its own small "embedder". Its output is the **sum** of up to three parts, then normalized to
the scale Qwen expects:

- **Column embedding**: says *which* column this is. It's initialized from Qwen's own word vectors for the column name (the
  mean of the vectors of the tokens in "Flight Distance"), then trained.
- **Value embedding**: a lookup table indexed by the feature's code. Each category, each rating level, each age, and each of
  3,300 Flight-Distance "routes" gets its own learned vector.
- **Numeric embedding** (Age, Flight Distance, both delays): the standardized number x goes through *periodic features*
  sin(2πf·x) and cos(2πf·x) at 32 learned frequencies f, then a small MLP (64 → 1,024). This is the same idea RealMLP uses so a
  network can resolve fine numeric differences.
- **RMSNorm × gain**: rescales the vector to RMS ≈ 0.030, the size of a typical Qwen word vector, so it enters the network like
  a normal token.

### How each column is coded

Vocabularies come from train + test features only (label-free).

| Columns | Value embedding (code) | Vocabulary | Numeric embedding |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Gender, Customer Type, Type of Travel, Class | category | 2, 2, 2, 3 | no |
| 13 service ratings (wifi … cleanliness) | rating level 0–5 | 6 each | no |
| Age | one code per distinct age | 75 | yes (standardized age) |
| Flight Distance | route id for every distance seen ≥ 3 times; rarer → "rare" code | 3,301 | yes (standardized log distance) |
| Departure / Arrival Delay | bucket {0, 1–5, 6–15, 16–30, 31–60, 61–120, >120, missing} | 8 each | yes (standardized log(1 + minutes)) |

Flight Distance gets both an ID and a number because in this dataset it behaves like a *route ID*: each distinct distance has
its own mix of passengers. The ID lets the model learn per-route effects; the number lets it share information between nearby
distances.

### Worked example: training row 0

| Column | Value | Code | Numeric x |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Gender | Female | 0 | – |
| Customer Type | Loyal Customer | 0 | – |
| Age | 36 | 29 | −0.217 |
| Type of Travel | Personal Travel | 1 | – |
| Class | Eco | 1 | – |
| Flight Distance | 694 | 436 | −0.594 |
| Inflight wifi / Time convenient / Online booking / Gate | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | – |
| Food / Online boarding / Seat comfort / Entertainment | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | – |
| On-board / Leg room / Baggage / Check-in / Cleanliness | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | – |
| Departure Delay / Arrival Delay | 0 / 0.0 | 0 / 0 | −0.289 / −0.281 |
| *Label* | *satisfaction = False* | target, never an input | |

These 21 codes and 4 numbers become 21 vectors of 1,024 numbers each, a 21 × 1,024 matrix that stands in for a "sentence".

## 3. Feeding the vectors into Qwen

Hugging Face models accept `inputs_embeds`: you can pass vectors directly instead of token ids, which skips Qwen's
word-embedding table. Q-FT builds the sequence like this:

1. **Shuffle the 21 feature tokens** into a fresh random order for every row, every training step.
2. **Append a learned CLS vector** as position 22. It's the model's "answer slot".
3. Qwen applies its usual rotary positions (0…21) and runs **causal attention**: each position sees only itself and earlier
   positions. So only the *last* position, CLS, sees all 21 features.
4. The final hidden state at CLS (1,024 numbers) goes through a `Linear(1024 → 1)` head, giving one logit.

> **Why the random order matters.** A causal transformer sees features one after another. With a fixed order, the model ties
> itself to that one sequence. Shuffling every row teaches it that order is meaningless (like a set) and acts as strong data
> augmentation. In our pilots the fixed order lost **0.0069 AUC** (0.9535 vs 0.9604).

## 4. LoRA: fine-tuning a big model by training a tiny add-on

Qwen3-0.6B has about 440M weights in its 28 layers. Instead of updating all of them, **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes
every original weight matrix W and learns a small correction next to it:

`output = W·x + (α / r) · B·(A·x)`

- **A** squeezes the input down to r = 16 numbers and **B** expands them back. Together B·A is a "rank-16" update to W.
- **B starts at zero**, so at step 0 the model is exactly pretrained Qwen. Training then moves only A and B. The scale
  α/r = 32/16 = 2.
- Adapters sit on all 7 projection matrices of every layer: attention q, k, v, o and MLP gate, up, down.
- **10.1M trainable LoRA weights** (about 2% of the backbone), plus 3.9M in the feature tokenizer and the CLS/head. The frozen
  0.6B weights still run in the forward and backward passes.

## 5. Training recipe

| Item | Setting |
|---|---|
| Data per fold | 559,708 outer-train rows (StratifiedKFold 5, seed 42); the held-out fold is only predicted |
| Backbone | Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base: 28 layers, width 1,024, 16 attention heads (8 key/value heads), MLP width 3,072 |
| Fine-tuning | LoRA rank 16 (α 32) on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down; backbone frozen otherwise |
| Loss | binary cross-entropy on the CLS logit |
| Optimizer | AdamW (fused). Learning rate 2e-4 for the LoRA adapters, 1e-3 for the tokenizer, CLS and head; no weight decay |
| Schedule | 3 epochs (3,279 steps of 512 rows), 3% linear warmup, then linear decay to 0 |
| Precision | bf16 autocast for the transformer, fp32 master weights; gradient clipping at 1.0 |
| Augmentation | new random feature order for every row at every step |
| Prediction | mean logit over 5 feature orders (the table's order + 4 random) |
| Cost | ~920 rows/s, 26 GB peak memory, ~52 min per fold on one A100 (5 folds in parallel on 5 GPUs) |

## 6. What we found

**Fold-0 pilots, 3 epochs each:**

| Variant | Fold-0 AUC | Takeaway |
|---|---:|---|
| **LoRA r16, pretrained Qwen** | **0.960444** | best |
| Random-init backbone (same architecture), full training | 0.960436 | pretraining adds nothing |
| Frozen backbone (only tokenizer + head train) | 0.959788 | a frozen LLM is already a decent feature mixer |
| Random column embeddings (no column names) | 0.958479 | names don't matter (compare full FT 0.958004) |
| Full fine-tune, learning rate 2e-5 | 0.958004 | learning rate too low for full FT |
| Fixed feature order | 0.953546 | shuffling is essential |

**All 5 folds:**

The 4.5 h isn't tuning time. It's training the final model: 5 folds × 8 seeds = 40 RealMLP fits (pytabkit RealMLP_TD_Classifier), each with n_ens=8, so 320 networks in total, about 7 min per fit on one A100.

Tuning was not a cold-start Optuna search. We started from two known-good parameter sets: our RealMLP params from S6E8 (1st place) and a public RealMLP setup. pytabkit defaults served as a reference. Then we screened a small hand-designed grid of 26 configs. Each config ran on 2 folds × 2 seeds (about 9 GPU-hours in total), with honest training: a 5% inner holdout of outer-train picks the best epoch, and the scored fold is only predicted. We used an AI coding assistant to run and analyse the grid.

Only one knob really mattered: plr_sigma, the scale of RealMLP's periodic numeric embeddings. Raising it from 0.94 (S6E8 set) to 32 gave about +5.5e-4 AUC. Flight Distance has about 3.5k distinct values and behaves like a route ID, so it needs fine resolution. It's the same effect as XGBoost improving with max_bin=4096. Epochs, learning rate, width, dropout, batch size and label smoothing were all within seed noise (±1e-4).

Final config: the S6E8 parameter set with n_epochs=20 and plr_sigma=32; everything else unchanged. In the feature-engineering table we reused these settings as is (no re-tuning on the 30-column view).

Much of the recent LB movement here comes in steps of 0.00001, so I measured how much of that is noise.

Method: I took the 124 public OOF pairs ([Chris Deotte's dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/cdeotte/s6e10-124-public-oof-and-test-predictions)), drew 200 random 60k-row slices of the labelled OOF (the public LB is 20% of test, about 60k rows), and recorded how much the AUC gap between two submissions moves from slice to slice. I did this for 136 pairs of single models and stacks.

Result: the noise of a public-LB gap depends almost only on how similar the two submissions are:

**sd(public gap) ≈ 0.0012 · √(1 − ρ)**, where ρ = rank correlation of the two test predictions (median relative error 2.5%)

| ρ | noise sd | 2-sd gain needs |
|---|---|---|
| 0.99999 | 0.000004 | 0.000008 |
| 0.9999 | 0.000012 | 0.000025 |
| 0.999 | 0.000039 | 0.000078 |
| 0.99 | 0.000124 | 0.000248 |

Example: the same 124-member stack at C=0.003 vs C=0.03 has a true OOF gap under 0.00001, and the public slice ranks the two the wrong way round about 30% of the time.

You can compute ρ from two submission files without any labels, so the notebook has a `lb_noise(sub_a, sub_b, lb_gap)` helper that tells you whether a gap you saw is signal or noise:
https://www.kaggle.com/code/korokke3/s6e10-is-your-0-00001-real-lb-noise-calculator

The private slice is 4× larger, so its noise is about half of the public noise. Picking finals by OOF CV (700k rows) is a much stronger test than the public LB.
