Team Farmcore, 4th place of ~10 200 teams. Corresponding author: [Iaroslav Pudovkin](https://www.kaggle.com/betmyex). Code: [github.com/B3tMy3x/farmcore-kaggriculture](https://github.com/B3tMy3x/farmcore-kaggriculture). Trained agent: [Kaggle Models](https://www.kaggle.com/models/betmyex/farmcore-kaggriculture-agent).

Our final agent is pure behavioral cloning: no search at play time, no self-play data. The biggest gain came from fixing the labels, not the model: retrained on what the engine executed instead of what players ordered, plus one feeding rule, the same network went from 3 to 23 wins of 24 against our previous best. The three main choices:

1. **We imitate what the engine executed, not what the player ordered.** Strong players over-order and let the engine silently drop the rest. Cloning those orders teaches a policy to issue empty orders.
2. **The whole turn comes out of one forward pass.** A transformer drafts every unit's job and every market decision at once, then a six-layer corrector reads that soft draft once and lets all decisions adjust to each other.
3. **Pretrain broadly, fine-tune narrowly, then average.** Pretrain on 67 top submissions, fine-tune on a single team, and average the weights of two such fine-tunes.

PPO improved our policy too, but per GPU-hour, data and pretraining paid at least ten times more (section 6). After the deadline we found a market mechanic we never modeled: the engine pairs the players' orders by position in the market list, so whoever lists a good first sells it first (+$4 or −$10 per unit). In replays it is worth up to $0.4–0.6k per game against the top 3; we never tested a fix on the ladder (section 5).

| | |
|---|---|
| final model, end to end | ≈5.5 A100-hours |
| training data | 8 583 replays of 67 top submissions, then 563 and 766 replays of one team |
| self-play games in the final model | 0 (the winner: ~8.3M) |
| hardware | 1–2 × A100-80GB provided by our university, plus free cloud compute |
| cost to us | $0 |
| evaluation | ~19k paired-seed games, on CPU |

**How to read the numbers.** A strong agent ends a game with about $100k. The engine is deterministic, so we compare two agents on the same seeds (usually 48): "+$X" is the mean per-game difference in final money, "44/48" means ahead on 44 of 48 seeds. *Margin* is our money minus the opponent's.

| | Common approach | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| Imitation target | Recorded player actions | State changes the engine actually applied |
| Turn generation | Independent per-unit outputs or autoregressive decoding | A draft of the whole turn, then a corrector over all decisions |
| After cloning | Large-scale PPO self-play | Broad pretraining, single-team fine-tuning, weight averaging |
| Checkpoint selection | Validation metrics or local win rate | Money on paired seeds |

## 1. What we imitate: executed trades, not orders

The engine executes a market order one unit at a time. When an order tries to sell from an empty shed or buy beyond the available money, it stops at the first unit that fails and silently drops the rest.

Many top players rely on this and over-order. Replaying the games of 15 top players showed how little of their orders executed:

A policy trained on recorded actions learns these empty orders, while at play time our decoder clips them to the real shed and budget: it is trained in one world and plays in another. The fix works with any deterministic engine:

1. Replay every game, feeding both players' recorded actions.
2. Hook the engine's commit function and log what executed: units sold, bought, hired.
3. Check that replayed money matches recorded money at every step; drop games that do not reproduce.
4. Use the executed changes as labels, and cancel round trips (selling an item and buying it back in the same turn).
5. Compute all input features from the same replayed record, so training and play see the same quantities.

Against our previous best, the clone won 3/24 games on raw orders, 12/24 on executed labels and 23/24 with the feed guard below.

**Rules for states the teacher never visited.** A clone eventually reaches states absent from its teacher's games. Our teacher always fed its animals its own wheat, so its data never had a hungry herd and an empty shed; the clone stalled there, and animals unfed for two days run away. Three rules derived from the game mechanics closed such gaps:

* *Feed guard:* each turn, buy exactly enough wheat to feed the animals not yet fed today.
* *Night-shed sell:* at night units dump their loads into the shed and the overflow is destroyed, so on each day's last turn we sell what would be lost (+$0.5k on average over five opponents).
* *End sell:* sell the whole shed on the final turn.

Six other "common sense" rules (more coops, capped wheat purchases, spreading units out) were neutral or negative. Even blocking requests larger than the shed lost money: the engine turns such a request into a harmless no-op, while a blocked unit wastes its turn.

## 2. How a turn is built: one pass, then a corrector

A turn is a plan, and a plan is easiest to fix when all of it is visible. So the network drafts the whole turn in one pass, then a corrector lets the decisions see each other and revise:

* **Input:** one token per own tile (100), per unit (up to 24), per product, crop and animal, plus a global token. The opponent's farm goes through its own encoder and a four-latent bottleneck.
* **Trunk:** nine transformer blocks. Each head has a learned 19×19 relative-position bias over the offset (dx, dy), shared across layers; removing it cost money.
* **Draft heads:** each unit gets a pointer to its target tile and an action. The market gets an open/closed gate and a quantity per item and order type, plus hiring and land. No head sees what the others decided: unit 3 doesn't know that unit 7 is heading for the same melon, and the sell head doesn't know what the units will drop into the shed this turn.
* **Movement:** a rule, not a prediction. Every teacher step we measured was a shortest-path move toward the unit's next job, so the network picks the tile and a rule takes the steps.
* **Corrector:** each unit gets its *intent*, the draft target distribution averaged over tile keys, and cross-attends to our tiles to see what lies on a contested target. Market tokens get the expected sells and buys and the shed as it will be at market time, after this turn's pickups and drop-offs; the global token gets the expected spend and revenue, computed explicitly. Six transformer layers run once over these 42 decision tokens (24 unit slots, 9 goods, 5 crops, 3 animals, 1 global), and the same heads give the final decisions.
* **Training:** end to end, with the loss only on final decisions, so the draft learns only through the corrector. The corrector reads the network's own soft draft, never the ground truth: a variant fed the true plan learned to trust it and lost in live play.

The policy has 21.5M parameters, about 16M at play time (the rest is a training-only value tower), and runs in FP32 PyTorch on two CPU threads, well within the 1 s limit. The case for this design is the error structure, not speed: the errors autoregression fixes (the right action given to the wrong unit) were only about a fifth of the clone's errors.

**What the corrector actually does.** It changes the target of 25% of units and the market orders in 74% of turns; without it, money drops from ~$100k to ~$14k and all 48 paired games are lost. But it does not do the job we designed it for: target collisions are as frequent after it as before (0.086 vs 0.088 per turn). Instead:

* in 17% of unit-turns the draft keeps the unit working its current tile and the corrector sends it elsewhere. The draft is a greedy "do the nearest job" policy, and the plan lives in the corrector;
* in the market it mostly closes gates: the draft opens 32% of sell gates, the final turn 14%;
* the draft is badly calibrated (expected calibration error 0.21 on sells). It is not a weaker policy but a feature map that the corrector reads.

**Where each decision is made.** With an early-exit form of the logit lens from LLM interpretability, we cut the trunk after k of 9 layers or the corrector after k of 6 and compare the turn with the full network's on 8 640 ladder states:

At play time we also subtract the training class priors from the logits (logit adjustment, β = 1): +$3.2k and 44/48 against the same weights with raw logits.

## 3. How it was trained: pretrain, fine-tune, average

One pooled corpus of many top players was worse than cloning a single team. A clone matched its teacher on 88% of unit actions, while top teams agreed with each other on only 66–68%: a pooled model mixes neighbouring decisions of different players, and its plans stop fitting together. Cloning the top-ranked player also underperformed: reactive players clone cleanly, long-horizon planners do not.

Splitting training into stages worked:

1. **Pretrain** on the relabeled games of many top teams.
2. **Fine-tune** on a single strong team: +$9.2k and 89/96 against our previous model, and clearly better than training on that team from scratch.
3. **Average the weights** of two fine-tunes that start from the same pretrain but use different submissions of that team. Reliably about +$1k over a parent; our best soup gained +$3.3k (46/48), and re-running the recipe with other seeds gave +$0.9k and +$1.1k.

Mixing weights works like mixing data of one team, not like mixing teams. Because both parents start from the same point and agree on about 80% of unit actions, averaging their weights behaves much like ensembling their logits, at no inference cost.

**What the soup actually does.** We ran the pretrain, both parents and the soup on the same 5 760 ladder states:

**How we chose checkpoints.** Whole-turn validation accuracy correlated negatively with money (rank correlation −0.86 over eight versions), and our best validation ever came from a data leak. So we selected only by paired-seed money, in the final week against a panel of 5–7 opponents, since strength was not transitive: some versions gained +$8k against one baseline and lost to others. Our worst bugs were train/play mismatches that never showed in validation; only step-by-step comparison with the engine caught them.

## 4. What the network learned (interpretability)

Shuffling one input group at a time in live games shows what the policy relies on:

**What the product tokens encode.** A sparse autoencoder, the standard tool for reading LLM activations (TopK, 1 024 features, 315k product tokens from 35k ladder states, 4.5% variance unexplained), splits the network's view of each good into readable features:

The feature directions are causally meaningful, though not strong levers. Pushing the milk token along a milk feature's direction, by twice the token's own norm, opens the milk sell gate on 58% of states instead of 3%; 20 random directions of the same size reach at most 8%. A fertilizer feature does the same, 18% → 51% (random: at most 22%). At shifts the size of the token itself the effect is small (milk 3% → 8%). Removing a single feature, though, rarely closes a gate: each decision is carried by several features at once. It is a cheap way to check what a cloned policy keys on before shipping it.

**It found the town's four-turn shop cycle on its own.** Strawberries, milk and wool are sold almost only on shop turns (sell probability 0.4–0.7, against under 0.1 on other turns), and sales rise with price and with stock in the shed:

**The opponent representation collapsed into one signal.** The four opponent latents have a cosine similarity of 0.993: the policy tracks the opponent mainly through the shared market, not through their board. The exception is livestock: buying cows and sheep takes finite, shared milk and wool demand away from the opponent. Disabling the corrector for livestock purchases cost $29k of margin, $26k of which went to the opponent.

## 5. Against the field

Margin per game of our final model against each top team, from two weeks of post-deadline ladder games:

The margins are tiny: in 64% of games the gap is under $2k on ~$100k, and in 29% it is smaller than the effect of changing a single move (replacing one move with `PASS` shifts the final money by a median $0.7–0.85k, with a stable sign for only ~24 turns). Among the top teams, places are decided by many near-coin-flips, which is also why per-move credit in RL is so expensive (section 6).

### Where we lose to the top 3

We replayed our 295 ladder games against the top 3 through the engine, logging every executed market unit and its price (money reconciles to the dollar). Each side sells ~$135k of goods per game, and our selling looks almost identical to the 1st place's: same hours, same batch sizes, same number of sales. The gap is in high-value goods (strawberries, milk, wool), and against the 1st place about half of it is price, not volume: the same units sold $2–3 cheaper.

Part of the reason is a mechanic we never modeled. The engine executes order *i* of one player together with order *i* of the other, unit by unit, and every unit sold moves the price down. So when both players sell the same good in the same turn (a collision), whoever put it earlier in their market list sells first:

Summed over these collisions, that is up to −$0.4–0.6k per game against each of the top 3. This is a replay estimate, not a causal effect: who lists a good first depends on the state of the game, and the opponent would also play differently against a different order. All three top teams sort their sells by price every turn (rank correlation of list position with price −0.58 to −0.62). Our decoder lists sells in a fixed order that starts with wheat, the cheapest good (−0.09), so the network could not compete for the slot. The only causal test we ran: sorting our sells by price gains +$216 ± 189 per game (69% of 48 paired seeds) against our older package, which sells in our order. Against teams that sort by price the gain could differ either way; we found this after the deadline and never tested it on the ladder.

## 6. RL worked; scaling the data worked far better

PPO on top of our imitation checkpoints, with the change in farm net worth as the reward, gained +$1.3k per game over its starting checkpoint (64/96 paired seeds, p = 1e-5), and an RL checkpoint was one of our ladder submissions. Our teammate's self-play runs of ~100k games each gave similar gains.

We dropped it because of compute. Per GPU-hour, data and pretraining paid at least ten times more than our best PPO run:

| | compute | gain |
|---|---|---|
| best PPO run (23 updates of 128 games) | ~2.8 A100-hours | +$1.3k |
| longest PPO run (260 updates) | ~30 A100-hours (estimated) | −$14k against the relabeled clone below |
| relabeling the corpus with executed trades | an afternoon of CPU | 3/24 → 23/24 against our previous best |
| fine-tuning the pretrained model on one team | 1.2 A100-hours | +$9.2k (89/96) |
| the whole final model | ≈5.5 A100-hours | 4th place |

Both final submissions are pure imitation; the RL loop is in the repository as a working tool. Rule of thumb for similar competitions: if the engine is deterministic and strong replays are public, relabel and clone first; PPO on top pays only with far more compute than we had.

Why PPO is so expensive here: at our batch size the per-move signal is mostly noise. Split one rollout of 128 games in two and compute the policy gradient on each half, and the cosine between the halves is 0.06 (−0.01 with shuffled advantages, 0.93 for a control target the policy itself determines). That matches the chaos probe in section 5: a move's true effect is worth $30–400 and visible for ~24 turns, while the final result moves by ±$1–2k for unrelated reasons. A net-worth reward also cannot see market sells: selling turns stock into cash of about the same value. PPO needs far larger batches, which is what teams with GPU fleets ran.

Compute reported by other top teams:

| | training hardware | notes |
|---|---|---|
| [1st place](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745073) | final 10M model: up to 17 A100 + 29 A30 (~7 + 20 on average); a parallel 20M model: up to 26 A100 more | ~8.29M self-play games |
| [pure BC, top 10](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745367) | one RTX 5090 | pretrain ≈50 min |
| [autoregressive SFT, top 10](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745036) | two RTX 4090 and an RTX 3090, a DGX Spark, rented Colab GPUs | final model trained from scratch on one Colab G4 |
| us | 1–2 university A100 + free cloud compute, $0 in total | final model ≈5.5 A100-hours, 0 self-play games |

Every pure-imitation team in the top 10 trained its final model on one to three cards. The GPU fleets bought the self-play scale that PPO needs.

## 7. What did not work

* Mixed multi-teacher corpora with teacher-style embeddings: weaker than one consistent teacher. Other teams gained from conditioning on team, version and outcome; we tried only a team embedding.
* Routing between expert models per decision head: gains against one opponent, losses against others.
* Feeding each unit its previous action: the clone learned to copy itself (−$25k for one teacher).
* All board tiles as corrector tokens: attention spread away from the units.
* Sampling actions instead of argmax: money within noise, fewer wins.
* Iterative multi-pass draft refinement: no gain over a single corrector step.

Thanks to the organizers for a genuinely interesting game, and to the teams at the top of the ladder: every one of our models learned by watching your games. This gold also made all of us Kaggle Competitions Masters. Thank you!

I spent my first day on a data audit instead of training anything, and honestly the punctuation table explains most of what makes this competition hard. Posting the numbers in case they save someone a day.

A few things I noticed:

Lab is almost readable from two columns. Claude and GLM love em dashes and only ever use straight quotes. GPT and Gemini are the opposite: curly apostrophes everywhere, straight quotes basically never. Gemini barely uses em dashes at all.

GLM looks like Claude on every single marker here. Which is probably why glm-5.3 and glm-5.3-flash are two of my three worst classes right now (recall 0.17 and 0.19). Punctuation can't separate them from Claude, so that has to come from word choice.

Siblings are flat. Inside OpenAI the em dash rate goes from 9% (gpt-6-astra) to 37% (gpt-5.6-luna), which is something, but not much. Inside Gemini the four models mostly differ on how often they use a curly apostrophe (6% to 31%). Everything else about the sibling problem lives somewhere other than punctuation.

On the error split: a plain TF-IDF (char 1-5 + word 1-2, lowercase=False) with logistic regression, validated with StratifiedGroupKFold on prompt_id, gets 0.345 balanced accuracy (CI 0.33 to 0.36, bootstrapped over prompts). If you only ask "did it get the lab right", the same predictions score 0.58, and 55% of all mistakes are the right lab, wrong model. I then added a char_wb affix view and about 80 hand-made typography and rhythm features (dash/quote variants, sentence length stats, type-token ratio) in a LightGBM and blended the three. That gets to 0.372 (CI 0.36 to 0.39), lab accuracy 0.61... and the within-lab share of errors actually goes UP to 58%. So the classical stuff is solving the easy lab problem and barely scratching the sibling problem.

Length matters more than I expected. Under 60 words the blend is at 0.27, over 160 words it's at 0.46. If your CV looks healthy, it's worth checking it by length bucket before trusting it.

Two things that did not work, since those are useful too. First-word habits aren't a tell here: every lab opens with "the" or "in" most of the time, so openers don't carry the signal some papers report. And the punctuation "rules" that look absolute in train (Gemini never using em dashes, Claude never using curly quotes) are exactly the kind of thing that breaks on freshly generated text, so I'm treating them as features to learn alongside everything else, not as hard filters.

For what it's worth, the top LightGBM features were comma rate, type-token ratio, word-length std, sentence-length std, capitalised-word rate and long-word rate. Vocabulary richness and rhythm, not any one mark.

All of this is grouped CV on the public train set only, 5 folds x 3 seeds, no external data. Happy to be corrected on any of it.

I’ve been experimenting with trajectory-based LoRA SFT for Gemma 4, but haven’t seen improved autonomous issue resolution so far. Looking through related work, I noticed that several prominent success stories use full-parameter fine-tuning for their main agent policies:
- SWE-Gym: the OpenHands policy experiments use full fine-tuning for the 7B, 14B and 32B models.
- SWE-smith: its main trajectory-training recipe uses full fine-tuning.
- SWE-Lego: explicitly uses full-parameter SFT.
- SWE-Protégé: reports that LoRA and QLoRA underperformed full SFT under the same data and evaluation protocol, although it does not provide the adapter configurations or comparison scores.
My own local experiments used Gemma 4 E4B with:
- 170 continuous teacher trajectories covering 62 training issues.
- LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, targeting both attention and MLP projections.
- Peak learning rate of 1e-4, trained through four epochs.
- Complete trajectories, supervising assistant responses while masking user/tool observations.
- Matching QAT-derived weights, tools and inference budgets for the Base/SFT comparison.
Training loss decreased and predictions on recorded training histories improved. However, autonomous execution did not beat Base on my small evaluation panel: Base solved 2/4 training cases and 1/8 development cases, while the best tested SFT checkpoints solved 1/4 and 1/8, respectively.
Observed failures included repeated searches, unsuccessful edits and poor recovery after tool errors. In a separate small overfitting experiment, the model could reproduce the correct teacher actions on two fixed histories, yet still failed when starting autonomously from the original buggy repository.
These are preliminary, small-sample results—not proof that LoRA is the cause. There are also positive LoRA examples, such as TQS. Still, I wonder whether low-rank adaptation can become a bottleneck when learning an entire coding policy, even when the recorded trajectories can be fitted.
Has anyone obtained consistent end-to-end gains over the unchanged Base model using LoRA SFT in this competition? Comparisons across ranks—or matched LoRA versus full fine-tuning—would be particularly useful. Please share training configurations and actual autonomous repair results if available.
I’m also exploring LoRA-based RL separately; the observations above concern SFT.

btw, i'm only interested in training part for this competition

text:
## Summary

My final agent (MXFMHF12D) finished 19th of 10,148 teams with a final score of 5,210.3. It is a behaviour clone of the teams that finished 1st, 3rd and 7th: M & M & P & Q, DSM and DECEM. Twelve small networks trained on their replays (and on older games in slots the agent does not play from) each score every move, the agent averages their probabilities, and three rules sell goods the engine would otherwise destroy. No RL went into it, and it does no search at play time.

Four things I measured that may be useful next to Farmcore's and DECEM's write-ups:

1. Pooling three teams that play the same four-quadrant plan beat a clone of M & M & P & Q alone against all seven opponents I tested.
2. Training from scratch and keeping the last epoch beat fine-tuning older networks and beat picking epochs by validation loss.
3. Averaging networks from families trained on different views of the data beat adding more networks of one family.
4. A local test that ranked my live files correctly still could not see where my clones lose.

## Data

For each teacher I downloaded the replays of its current submissions through Kaggle's episode list endpoint, every 30 minutes on the last day. By the morning of 30 September I had 653 M & M & P & Q games, 578 DSM games and 549 DECEM games, plus about 1,900 games from 12 older M & M & P & Q submissions.

Each training record is one teacher seat in one game, seen from that seat. The labels are the orders the teacher requested, with market quantities clipped to 30.

One bug mattered. BUY_PRODUCT orders above 30 were not clipped, so any record that contained one was dropped. DSM and DECEM often buy wheat in bulk around day 10, so until a fix on the last day more than half of their games (316 of 589) never reached training. Farmcore relabelled to the trades the engine actually executed, and that is what I would add first.

## Model

Each network is a small CNN with 898,498 parameters. The board runs through three residual blocks with the global features added to every tile, and each unit's 132 features join at the unit head. The unit head picks each unit's verb and quantity, and an autoregressive market head writes up to ten orders after seeing what the units will do to the shed. Every network trains from scratch with AdamW (batch 256, peak learning rate 1e-3) and a OneCycle schedule that anneals to zero, for 10 epochs at first and 16 later, and I keep the last epoch.

The trainer has three version slots. The teachers' newest games sit in the slot the agent plays from, and older games (Boey's, and older M & M & P & Q submissions in some families) sit in the other two, as far as I can reconstruct from the trainer. The network learns from old games without being asked to play like them, the same idea as DECEM's date buckets.

**Decoding.** Units take the argmax of the averaged distribution, with a legality mask so a later unit sees what earlier units took. Purchases need more care: plain argmax never makes a purchase the teacher makes with a 20 % chance per step. Error diffusion fixes that. An accumulator adds the expected purchases each step and buys when it reaches one. On my first clone, error diffusion and a later refinement were worth 15k to 20k coins per game; the final file uses plain error diffusion. DECEM describes a similar accumulator.

## What mattered

All results are paired: a candidate and a control play the same towns against the same opponent, with a dithered opening, and I report the mean difference in final margin. ± is one standard error. A final bank is roughly 90k to 160k coins.

**Train from scratch, and keep the last epoch.** Eight fresh networks beat my live clone of Boey (23rd) by 11.0k per game summed over three opponents. Fine-tuning older networks on the same data gave 0.9k, or 3.5k with the newest games weighted up. The same eight networks at their lowest-validation-loss epoch gave 7.4k. The agent plays argmax, so validation loss is the wrong yardstick.

**Pool three teachers that share a plan.** DSM and DECEM play the same four-quadrant skeleton as M & M & P & Q: land, hires, a large wheat ring and animals. Alone they had too few games for a good clone. Pooled with M & M & P & Q, they beat the M&M-only clone by 3.9k ± 0.8k summed over three standard opponents, and by 1.2k to 4.1k against four others. Farmcore found that pooling many top players was worse than cloning one team, and they explain it by plans that stop fitting together. My three teachers share one plan, which may be why pooling worked; I did not measure how often they agree.

**Families beat more networks.** A family is a set of networks trained with one recipe on one view of the data. More networks within a family did nothing measurable, while a second family lifted my local score V1 (see Validation) from 0.705 to 0.784. My final file (Final A) averages three families, MXNF2 ×3, MXNM ×6 and MXHF ×3, and scored 0.879 on 700 towns, against 0.847 for my other final file (Final B) and 0.700 for a clone of the teachers' newest games. Part of the lead is selection: the same recipe with new seeds scored 0.835, and the two final files ended 24 points apart in the final standings.

**Three small rules.** OVERFLOW sells what will not fit in the shed at midnight, ENDGAME stops investments that cannot pay back and sells everything at the end, and ENDRUSH sends units carrying goods to the shed before the last step. Leaving one out cost 1,722, 676 and 252 coins per game, summed over three opponents.

## Validation

**Dither the opening.** Days 0 to 2 have no shops and weeds start at step 48, so two deterministic programs play the same opening in every town, and a test measures one opening plus noise. Against a dithered opponent, a null change read −677 ± 1,290 on 50 towns instead of −11,389 ± 2,140 on 15. Seeing 1k at two standard errors then takes about 340 towns.

**V1** = ½ × mean(win rate against a strong M&M copy, win rate against the M&M-only clone) + ½ × win rate against the pooled clone. Across five live files its two copy cells correlated 0.93 and 0.94 with the live ratings, and the final standings ordered my two final files the way V1 did.

**What V1 missed.** Its references are my own clones, so they share my blind spots. In 18 replays against teams rated above 2,550, three of the six losses came from too few strawberries and too little milk, and in wins and losses alike my agent left 16 to 22 more animal-days unfed per game than M & M & P & Q did against the same opponents. In M & M & P & Q's own positions it picks their exact action 0.91 to 0.99 of the time, but in free play only 0.26 to 0.40 of positions match from day 6. The money is lost in states the teacher never visits.

## What did not work

| Idea | Result |
|---|---|
| PPO from an early clone (6.0M steps) | its own sampled metric rose 3.0k; the deterministic agent I ship lost 23.3k |
| Fine-tuning a clone on its own best rollouts | −5.0k |
| DSM's recorded opening, then my clone | −22.5k against one opponent |
| Sending units to rescue drying plants | −1,756 against one opponent |

The PPO run was small, so it says nothing about PPO at the scale the winners used.

## Thanks

Thanks to Kaggle for the game, and to M & M & P & Q, DSM and DECEM, whose games my networks learned from. Thanks also to Boey, whose games taught my earlier clones and are still in the final networks' training data, and to the authors of the public notebooks I submitted or forked:

- Thomas Tschinkel's [Public State Router](https://www.kaggle.com/code/thomastschinkel/kaggriculture-93-8-win-rate-public-state-router)
- WUZB's [v15stack](https://www.kaggle.com/code/wzhengbiao/kaggriculture-v15stack-submit)
- Ahmed Berat Özer's [V57](https://www.kaggle.com/code/ahmedberatozer/kaggriculture-v57-funding-order-invariant)
- prvsiyan's [The Moon Counts Melons](https://www.kaggle.com/code/prvsiyan/kaggriculture-frontier-the-moon-counts-melons) and [The Soil Remembers Rain](https://www.kaggle.com/code/prvsiyan/kaggriculture-frontier-the-soil-remembers-rain), whose controller builds on haideptry's [The 2965 Master Hybrid Engine](https://www.kaggle.com/code/haideptry/the-2965-master-hybrid-engine)

Using daily PM2.5 aggregate data sourced from OpenAQ across six major urban centers in Pakistan over a 12-month window, I evaluated ambient air quality against the 2021 WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines. 

The findings present a critical look at regional baseline pollution:

* **Faisalabad Outpaces Lahore:** Faisalabad recorded the highest yearly mean at 119.6 µg/m³ (representing ~24x the WHO annual guideline), with zero days meeting the 24-hour safe threshold of 15 µg/m³.
* **Persistent Lahore Baseline:** Lahore recorded a yearly mean of 103.8 µg/m³ (~21x annual guideline) with 0 clean days, aligning closely with regional winter temperature inversion traps.
* **The Peshawar Outlier:** Often overlooked in mainstream discourse, Peshawar ranked third worst (91.5 µg/m³), displaying winter medians closely tracking industrial plains.
* **Year-Round vs. Seasonal Spikes:** While winter months see monthly medians soar past 200 µg/m³, summer medians consistently hover ~3x above safe thresholds, indicating a persistent, year-round industrial and vehicular baseline.

**Data Science Challenge:**
Since these metrics rely on low-cost sensor networks rather than reference-grade monitors, humidity calibration remains a major hurdle. How do you typically adjust low-cost particulate sensor bias in high-humidity regional datasets?

I'm Yuan800, a high school junior, and this was my first time leading a team in a Kaggle competition. All the rented compute for our whole competition, GPU and CPU, came to **$59.78**. Each of our final models was trained from scratch on one rented RTX 5090, and the larger one took about 4.5 hours. Our final agents use no self-play and no RL, and every evaluation ran on CPU. This post explains how our plain behaviour-cloning (BC) agent got into the gold range, and what we learned on the way.

## 1. What we did

For most of the competition we built rule-based agents: hand-written schedulers, route splicing, opening counter-play, and planner + executor programs. They got us into the upper part of the board but stalled there. When we analysed our replays, the problem was always the same. We could copy *what* the top teams built, but our executors lost a large share of the throughput doing it.

In the last two days we went back to BC. We trained a Transformer on replays of top games and added a thin rule layer at inference time. Both of our final submissions, Final-192 and Final-256, come from this pipeline.

*Figure 1. Our training and inference pipeline. Blue parts are learned, green parts are hand-written rules.*

## 2. Why BC worked this time

We had tried BC in August. Our model matched over 99% of common actions and still played badly. Three things had to change.

- **The action language had to survive the round trip.** In one early experiment, simply re-encoding quantities through our converter, without any training, turned an expert that won every game into one that lost every game. This time, before training anything, we checked that converting replays into labels and decoding the model's outputs back into game actions round-trips exactly.
- **Invalid requests are masked, not taught.** A raw request that the engine turns into PASS is removed from the loss. It is not used as a PASS label.
- **The whole team is decided together.** One decoder pass predicts every worker's action and an ordered list of market orders, so later orders can take into account the cash that earlier ones use.

## 3. Our model

A single Transformer reads the whole game state. In one pass it outputs an action for every unit and an ordered list of market orders. Final-192 and Final-256 differ mainly in width; they have 4.0M and 7.0M parameters. At inference, a shadow resolver commits orders one at a time against cash, seeds and shed space. An endgame routine then brings goods home and sells them.

## 4. Choosing the model by games, not by loss

Validation loss did not tell us which checkpoint was stronger. We played every candidate against our submitted Final-192 on the official engine, with both seat assignments. Most of the 256-wide run lost almost every game. The checkpoint with the lowest validation loss finished last in a round robin of four late 256 checkpoints plus Final-192 (32 fresh seeds, both seats for every pairing). Only the final checkpoint beat Final-192. We froze it and confirmed it on 64 seeds that had never been used for selection: **92 wins, 36 losses**.

*Figure 2. Win rate of our Final-256 checkpoints against Final-192. Each blue point is 64 games. The orange point is the frozen final model on fresh seeds, with a 95% bootstrap interval.*

Our explanation is the usual problem with BC. The loss measures fit on the expert's states, but a full game makes the policy recover from states that *its own* actions create, for 719 decisions in a row. t fuku's team saw the same thing in [their writeup](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745783). In their runs, several seeds of the same recipe reached the same validation loss, yet won anywhere from 3 to 23 of 40 games against their reference.

## 5. What did not work

**RL on top of BC.** We tried KL-constrained post-training. It improved the sampled policy and made our deployed argmax policy worse. In one case, a tiny shift flipped the farmer's choice at hour 44 from SOUTH to PASS. In every one of the 64 games, the first decision where the two policies differed was this one, and the candidate went 25–3–36 (wins–draws–losses) against its own base. When the deployed policy is greedy, a small average KL is not the same as a small change in behaviour.

*Figure 3. Action probabilities at the first divergence. The axis starts at 48%.*

**Fine-tuned branches and weight averaging.** Both of our branches had lower validation loss than the base and were individually weaker than it. Their average was weaker too.

## 6. Why our Final-256 could not beat Final-192 on the ladder

Locally, Final-256 beat Final-192 92–36 on fresh seeds. On the ladder it consistently rated below Final-192, and Final-192 is the version holding our score. The overall win rate was not the problem. Over the whole evaluation period Final-256 won 543 of 993 games and Final-192 won 529 of 1,000. What hurt Final-256 was a handful of almost one-sided matchups against strong teams ranked close to us. Final-192 played the same teams nearly evenly:

| Opponent | Final-192 | Final-256 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Majkel1337 | 24–28 | 1–57 |
| Luca | 23–29 | 7–48 |
| Boey | 18–23 | 6–29 |
| KawattaTaido | 22–31 | 1–26 |

*Wins–losses over the whole evaluation period.*

In Bradley–Terry-style rating, losing that reliably to opponents with similar ratings costs more than extra wins against weaker teams bring back. Once we corrected for opponent strength, our own estimate put Final-192 slightly above Final-256. To find out why, we sampled 80 replays of both versions against the same Majkel and Luca submissions. The town matters a lot here, so we split games by whether the town had a wool shop. Against Majkel, in towns without a wool shop (16–18 sampled games per version), Final-256's median final cash was 102.5k against 103.4k for Final-192, while Majkel finished with 114.7k against Final-256 and 99.3k against Final-192. Final-256 was further ahead on day 12, and the gap opened from day 15 onwards. In those towns Final-256 was not a worse farmer; it was a weaker competitor in the shared market and left more money for the other side. In wool-shop towns (only 6–8 games each), Final-256 also earned less itself (106.7k against 122.8k), so this is a direction, not a settled result. Against Luca, in towns without a wool shop, Final-256 earned about 7k less and Luca about 2.6k more. We could not pin the effect on one product, because with different seeds, the shops in each town dominate the product mix.

Our local test had only one opponent identity, Final-192 itself, and the two models share most of their training data. So the 92–36 tells us how 256 does against 192's habits, not against other styles. Next time we would check each candidate's record against the teams around us, and against the opponents our current version struggles with, before choosing the final two. We would also track our own money and the opponent's money separately, not just the margin.

This cost us more than our own rating. Between 3 and 14 October, by the per-game score changes the ladder reported, Majkel gained about 202 points from games against our two versions, mostly against Final-256, while its total rise over that period was about 113 points.

## 7. Limitations

**Ablations.** We did not have the compute to measure how much each rule (masks, resolver, endgame) contributed. That is the main open question we leave.

## Team contributions

- @yuan800: led the project; built our pipeline, training and evaluation.
- @jacqueszhelinzhang: the theoretical groundwork for our behaviour-cloning architecture.

## Acknowledgements

We used Claude Code as an assistant for replay analysis, debugging and running evaluations. Most of our CPU evaluations ran on an 8-core cloud server provided by Grok Bot.

Thanks to the hosts for the [daily top-episodes datasets](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kaggle/kaggriculture-episodes-index), which were the main source of our training data, and to every team whose replays we learned from (especially M & M & P & Q, whose games we weighted most). Thanks also to [nikital7](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nikital7/4000x-environment-speedup-kaggriculture) for the public notebook "4000x environment speedup", and to [destbreso](https://www.kaggle.com/code/destbreso/kagsim-the-engine-at-2000-episodes-per-second) for packaging it as `kagsim`. A fast engine that matches the official one on well-formed actions let us screen our earlier rule-based agents on a small CPU budget. All model-selection games in this post ran on the official engine.

We're busy with Q1 benchmark exams right now, so our code will be cleaned up and released later. Sorry for the wait!

text:
Hi all! I'm currently at the top of the public LB (early days, it will move), and these are my notes from the **first two days**, for newcomers. Sections 1-4 need no extra data or GPU. Metric: balanced accuracy over 18 classes (chance about 0.056). Start with the [official getting-started thread + Discord (749382)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749382).

**Pitfalls:** random K-fold, "cleaned" text, test-layout tricks that only work in CV, ignoring short passages, bf16 on T4, no internet at submission.

### 1. Group your folds by prompt

All 18 models answer each of the 150 train prompts once (2,699 rows; one prompt lacks one model). [Random vs grouped CV (749593)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749593) showed random folds mislead (0.217 vs 0.369, LB 0.355), and my TF-IDF runs agree: only `StratifiedGroupKFold` with `groups=prompt_id` tracked the LB.

Why is random CV *pessimistic*? Training passages sharing a validation passage's topic all come from the other 17 models, so topic words pull predictions toward wrong labels. Grouped folds keep prompts unseen, like the test.

### 2. CPU baseline code

Char + word TF-IDF + logistic regression: **grouped CV 0.343 (the snippet below prints 0.3426 with sklearn 1.9.1), public LB 0.353**. Character-level details carry signal, so keep the text as given (`TfidfVectorizer` lowercases by default):

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.sparse import hstack
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

tr = pd.read_csv('/kaggle/input/competitions/name-that-llm/train.csv')
y, oof = tr['model'].values, np.empty(len(tr), dtype=object)
cfgs = [dict(analyzer='char', ngram_range=(1, 5), max_features=300_000),
        dict(analyzer='word', ngram_range=(1, 2), max_features=200_000, token_pattern=r'(?u)\b\w+\b|[^\w\s]')]
cv = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for trn, val in cv.split(tr, y, groups=tr['prompt_id']):
    vs = [TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, lowercase=False, min_df=2, **c) for c in cfgs]
    Xtr = hstack([v.fit_transform(tr.text.iloc[trn]) for v in vs]).tocsr()
    Xva = hstack([v.transform(tr.text.iloc[val]) for v in vs]).tocsr()
    oof[val] = LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=3000).fit(Xtr, y[trn]).predict(Xva)
print('grouped CV:', balanced_accuracy_score(y, oof))
```

Swap in `StratifiedKFold` to see the gap.

### 3. A trick that backfired

I clustered test passages into likely prompts and used Hungarian assignment (`scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment`) so each model appears at most once per cluster: **+~0.10** in grouped CV (up to 18 answers per prompt). On the public LB:

- plain TF-IDF: 0.353
- plus clustering + Hungarian: 0.344
- plus per-cluster log-prob centering (subtract the cluster mean per class): 0.329

One drop may be noise, but CV promised +0.10. My read: the hidden test likely has few passages per prompt; a CV that simulates the test is only as good as that guess. [Test-time grouping (750213)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750213) also saw a smaller-than-simulated gain.

### 4. Short passages are hardest

Passages run ~40-250 words; short ones are much harder. Check your OOF by length:

```python
words = tr.text.str.split().str.len()
print(pd.Series(oof == y).groupby(pd.cut(words, [0, 60, 120, 180, 1000]), observed=True).mean())
```

### 5. Fine-tune an LLM (inference fits the free 2xT4)

With no extra data, Qwen3-14B-Base + LoRA r16 (all linear layers), a classification head, 3 epochs and `max_len` 384 gave **fold-0 CV 0.443, public LB 0.466** (TF-IDF: 0.353; public LoRA notebooks score higher). I trained outside Kaggle; inference on 2xT4:

- T4 has no bf16: use fp16. A 14B (~27.6 GiB) fits across both GPUs with `device_map="auto"` and ~14 GiB `max_memory` each.
- Merge LoRA into the base first (no peft overhead).
- Sort texts by length (max ~360 tokens, so 384 suffices): ~0.25 s/passage at batch 8, ~17-20 min for ~4,000 test rows.
- Attach weights as a Kaggle dataset.

### 6. Extra data: free options first

More passages from the 18 models help ([the generated-data debate (749447)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749447)). Free, public sets: [18-model wide response corpus (749629)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749629), [extra Claude passages (750224)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750224), [helper dataset (750267)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750267). Still open: rules on self-generated API data ([749613](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749613)) and the Kaggle Benchmarks free quota ([750038](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750038)).

Next read: [a beginner's journey from TF-IDF to LoRA notebooks (750230)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750230). Thanks to all linked authors; questions and corrections welcome!

text:
Thanks to Kaggle and the hosts for Kaggriculture. The game looks simple, but the shared market makes it hard. And thanks to the top teams, especially **DSM**, **M & M & P & Q** and **Victor @ Tufa Labs**. Their ladder games were our training data, so this solution is partly theirs.

**TL;DR.** For three weeks we built rule-based agents, planners and RL sale-timing policies, and they plateaued around 2,550-2,800. In the last four days we switched to **closed-loop behavioural cloning (BC)**: per-unit imitation of the top teams' ladder games, iterated on a single **RTX 5070 (12 GB)**. The CNN generations and the final fine-tunes ran on the 5070; the final ViT-style trunk was pre-trained on a Colab A100. The final agent is a hybrid ViT clone fine-tuned on DSM's tomato-always versions, with a small tomato top-up wrapper. Its final ladder score was **2807.4**.

---

## 1. Weeks 1-3: hand-built agents (subs 1-66)

Briefly, because most of it was beaten later:

- **Rules plus overlays.** We started from a public V37-lineage agent and layered on sale-timing, feed/fertilizer, opening guards and terminal planners.
- **An exact C++ port of our agent.** It passed two gates (zero action mismatches over 23 Python games) and runs **817 games/s** on 12 CPU threads, against about 0.01 games/s per core in Python. With it we trained a **REINFORCE sale-horizon table over 4.3M games**. That made sub 22/23, which reached 2801 on the mid-September ladder.
- **Route planners and VRP crews.** These included a closed-loop farm simulator with vehicle routing, route bandits and ridge-regression route tables.

What we learned from those weeks:

1. **The route (what you grow, and when you buy land and animals) is worth far more than the market layer.** We tested eleven market-layer levers, and every one was refuted.
2. **Replaying tapes is biased.** A recorded rival does not react to you, so a tape evaluation is only valid when the agent you substitute plays like the one the tape was recorded against.
3. **Mirror games are decided by who sells first.** Any fixed sale horizon loses once it is copied. A reactive lead detector, and then the RL table, beat every fixed horizon.
4. **We could not hand-build what the top teams did.** An exact cash audit showed DSM about **+$8.9k per game** ahead of us after controlling for shop luck. We tried tape executors, DSM-plan executors and a reactor on our planner, and none of them closed the gap.

## 2. The switch: per-unit closed-loop BC

Earlier "clones" replayed open-loop tapes of recorded games, so execution kept breaking. We made the policy itself the clone: **every turn, every unit (farmer and each hand) picks an action from a network that sees the current state.**

### Data

- We pulled top-team ladder replays through the Kaggle API, each with its seed and both seats' actions.
- A **seat-game** is one player's side of one game, so a game has two. We trained only on the seats played by the teams we were cloning. The opponent's farm is part of the observed state, but its actions are never training targets.
- Every game is **re-simulated exactly** in our fastsim (Python, later the C++ bridge). A game is kept only if the replayed money matches the recorded money (1644/1644 seat-games for the first DSM set).
- The data grew from **1.6k DSM seat-games** (v1) to **10.3k seat-games from the top ~30 teams** (data6), which is about 4.5M turns in the "latest agents" subset.

### Model

- **v1-v4 (CNN):** a residual CNN over the 10×10 farm. Tile classes are embedded (ours and the opponent's), plus 12 numeric channels and a global vector: hour, day, cash, shed, seeds, prices, market inventory, shops, a team/style slot and carried goods.
  - **Unit head:** the trunk feature at the unit's tile, the pooled trunk, the globals, the unit index and its inventory → 47 action tokens.
  - **Market head:** 21 order keys × 18 count buckets. Each key (e.g. `SELL MILK`, `BUY_SEED WHEAT`, `HIRE`) is its own 18-way classification over order sizes, where bucket 0 means "no order". We use classification rather than regression because order sizes are bursty, and most turns place no order at all.
  - **Loss:** cross-entropy on the unit actions plus cross-entropy on the market buckets (averaged over the 21 keys), with label smoothing 0.02.
- **ViT trunk:** a transformer over the 100 tile tokens.
- **worker_hybrid (final trunk):** two local convolutions, then attention over tile tokens plus explicit **worker tokens** (position, identity, inventory). Width 256, 6 layers.

- **Decoding is parallel, not autoregressive.** The trunk runs once per turn, and each unit's head reads that shared trunk with its own position, index and inventory. All units decode independently in that one pass, so no unit sees what another unit chose this turn. Two units can therefore claim the same harvest or feed (see section 6 for why we left that alone).
- **Inference:** a plain numpy forward pass with fp16 weights base64-encoded into a single `main.py` (about 5.6 MB). Parity with PyTorch is about 1e-6. A turn takes 20 ms for the CNN and 73 ms for the ViT locally, against the 1 s actTimeout.

### The decoder mattered more than the network

The first trained build finished the season on **$0**. The network was fine; the wrapper around it was not:

1. **Calibrated market thresholds.** Argmax never fires rare orders such as `BUY_LAND` or `HIRE`. Each market key now fires when P(count > 0) exceeds a per-key threshold, calibrated so the clone's held-out firing rate matches the teacher's.
2. **A sell-what-arrives clamp.** DSM sells the same turn it delivers, so at observation time its shed shows 0. SELL counts must be clamped to shed stock **plus goods PLACEd or DROPped this turn**. Without this, the clone hoarded milk and wool.
3. **A legal-op mask, a PLANT cap at seeds in stock, and a last-day dump.** The mask runs at inference only. Before the argmax, every op that is illegal for that unit on its tile this turn has its logit set to −1e9. Training sees the teacher's actions unmasked.

With those fixes, the same weights went from $0.1k to $75.6k in DSM's recorded worlds after 2 epochs. A few epochs later the clone made **more money than DSM itself** in DSM's own hold-out worlds (v1 at epoch 9: $128k against DSM's $121k over 16 worlds):

That benchmark keeps the opponent's recorded actions fixed, so it is a fidelity check, not proof that the clone was stronger than DSM (section 4 covers this bias). The closed-loop results are what convinced us. The first upload (v2f) went 24/26 on the ladder with a +$31k mean margin. Locally it beat our best hand-built agent **24/24 at +$19.6k per game**.

## 3. Training: an RTX 5070, plus Colab for the big trunks

All the CNN generations and the final fine-tunes were trained on one consumer GPU in a Windows desktop. The ViT and worker_hybrid sweeps were too slow on a 12 GB card, so we pre-trained those trunks on a Colab A100 and then fine-tuned and evaluated them on the 5070. The times below come from the training logs:

| model | data | epochs | wall-clock | where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 CNN 128×6 | 1.1M DSM turns | 16 | 36 min | RTX 5070 |
| v2 (+carried goods) | 1.2M turns | 16 | 40 min | RTX 5070 |
| v3 CNN 160×8 | 1.2M turns | 20 | 73 min | RTX 5070 |
| v4 top-20 teams | 3.5M turns | 12 | 117 min | RTX 5070 |
| v4d (DSM fine-tune) | 1.2M turns | 6 | 21 min | RTX 5070 |
| ViT / worker_hybrid sweeps | 7-10k seat-games | 12 | hours | Colab A100 |
| **dsmT (final fine-tune)** | 219 DSM seat-games | 3 (and 6) | **3.5 min** (3 epochs) | RTX 5070 |

What we learned about the hardware:

- **One GPU job at a time.** Running two GPU-batched harnesses together left half the games with an agent that never acted (bank stuck at $3,000), including the control.
- **The 12 GB card pages at ViT batch 1024** once anything else holds memory, which made training about 25× slower. We used a smaller batch or Colab.
- **Under Windows WDDM, each model call costs about 18 ms regardless of batch size**, so on this machine batching across games matters more than model size.
- **Pin BLAS to one thread** in evaluation workers. OpenBLAS threading made our small conv matmuls 2.5× slower.

### Architecture sweep

On the same data, features, heads and 12 epochs, **spatial attention beat temporal context by a wide margin.** Nearly all the gain from history comes from the previous action alone.

The held-out loss did not always predict closed-loop strength. A DSM-only fine-tune of the ViT had *lower* loss (0.194) but lost about $4k per game. **We judged every model by games, not by loss.**

## 4. Evaluation: fast, paired and on the right worlds

The bottleneck was always evaluation, not training.

- **GPU-batched gauntlet.** Worker processes play games as threads, and one GPU forward per build serves every waiting game (full fp32, TF32 off, because TF32 broke parity). **48 games take 101 s instead of 13 minutes**, and 45/48 games match the numpy path's money exactly.
- **Pinned ladder worlds.** A replay's `info.seed` reproduces the game exactly, so we replay *our real ladder losses* with the rival's recorded actions pinned and swap in a candidate. This is how we found the tomato gap below.
- **Why pinned worlds are still usable, despite the tape bias from section 1.** The pinned rival is open-loop. Once our candidate changes the shared market, the rival keeps selling into prices it never saw. That makes absolute pinned scores unreliable. We only used pinned worlds to compare two candidates, both close to the agent the tapes were recorded against. Because both sides of that comparison inherit the same bias, the paired difference stays meaningful while the market changes only a little. We also watched for open-loop artifacts. One MMPQ fine-tune scored +$24k per game pinned, but 54 of its pinned rival tapes crashed once the market diverged, so we threw it out. Pinned worlds were a screen, and closed-loop head-to-head games were the gate.
- **Teacher hold-out worlds.** These are the teacher's own post-training ladder games. Both pinned and head-to-head wins can be artifacts (that MMPQ fine-tune also won 75% head-to-head, yet was not a faithful clone), so the teacher's own held-out worlds were our fidelity check.
- **Count seeds, not games.** Every head-to-head seed is played twice with the seats swapped. Shop unlocks and weed spawns come from the seed, and the game treats the two seats the same. So when both agents play the same way in both games, the seat-swapped game mirrors the first and each agent's money comes out identical. That happened in about 70% of seeds between our near-identical clones. With 24 games you have about 12 independent worlds, not 24.
- **Gate rule.** Before any upload, the candidate must win the incumbent's ladder losses and post a clear head-to-head win rate against the incumbent.

## 5. The last gap: tomatoes

We audited 86 ladder games against the ~2800 tier. Our clone matched or beat them on every product except one:

The top teams started tomatoes late (median opponent tomato plants: 0 by day 14, 8 by day 17, 11.5 by day 20) and sold them at about $113. Our clone came from DSM versions that did not grow tomato, so it never started.

- **R4 wrapper.** If the opponent has at least 4 tomato plants between days 13 and 20, swap the clone's `PLANT WHEAT` to `PLANT TOMATO`, with a cap of 10 and a $1,500 cash guard. On 40 real tomato-opponent ladder worlds it scored **+$2.2k per game paired, with 7 losses flipped to wins and 0 wins flipped to losses.** Early tomato (from day 8) starved cash on days 8-10 and *lost* $6-9k per game.
- **Wrapper tuning hit a local optimum.** Other caps and triggers all landed within ±$230 of R4.
- **dsmT, the final model.** DSM's newest versions grow tomato in 100% of games, so we fine-tuned worker_hybrid on only those **219 seat-games** (lr/4, 3 epochs, **3.5 min on the 5070**). Validation unit loss went from 0.217 to 0.141. On its own, dsmT beat the wrapper agent (worker_hybrid + R4) by **+$2.4k per game** on 212 pinned ladder worlds, almost all of it in tomato worlds.
- **`_R4a`, the additive top-up.** R4 rewrites the network's choices: it turns `PLANT WHEAT` into `PLANT TOMATO` and limits tomato seed stock. That would fight a model that already wants tomato. `_R4a` uses the same trigger (opponent has 4 or more tomato plants on days 13-20), but it never edits or limits the network's own tomato buys and plants. It only adds tomato when the network's own plan is still under the cap. We kept it as a safety net because dsmT sometimes starts too late. In one head-to-head game it planted its first tomato on day 18, with only 4-6 plants. dsmT with `_R4a` beat R4 61% head-to-head and flipped 6 of R4's 12 losses on R4's own ladder worlds.
- **dsmT6e_R4a, the best final sub.** It is the same recipe at 6 epochs. Its validation loss is *worse* (0.150), but it went 70% head-to-head against R4 and 24/40 in DSM's held-out seat (R4 21/40). It ended at **2807.4**.

The lesson is that **a crop strategy has to come from the plan (the teacher), not from a wrapper.** As the main mechanism, the wrapper only patched the symptom: R4 alone hit a local optimum within ±$230. Switching the teacher was worth +$2.4k on top of that. In the final agent the wrapper is demoted to a small safety net on top of a policy that already grows tomato.

## 6. What did not work

| idea | result |
|---|---|
| Unit-coordination masks (dedupe units claiming the same fertilizer, harvest or feed) | −$42k to −$89k per game. The clone learned DSM's own collisions, and "fixing" them pushes it off-distribution. |
| Relabelling engine no-ops as PASS in training | 62% fewer no-ops, no score change |
| Single-team fine-tunes (MMPQ, Victor) / playing in a non-DSM style slot | −$3k to −$4k per game, despite better loss on that team's games |
| Mixing all top-20 teams with a style slot (v4) | no better than DSM-only |
| Weight soup (0.5·base + 0.5·fine-tune) | loss in between, but 25-38% head-to-head |
| Logit ensemble of 3 fine-tunes | +$0.4-0.7k per game, but no extra wins, and 3× slower (321 ms per turn) |
| Head-only PPO on the BC policy (frozen trunk, exact legal-set log-probs) | tied the base (+$36 ± $596) |
| Sale horizon by rival class, land-buying wrapper, sheep/goose annexes, melon races | all flat or negative |

## 7. Takeaways

1. **If move-level data from a stronger agent exists, clone it per unit and in closed loop first.** We spent weeks hand-building executors for plans that a 40-minute BC run on a consumer GPU learned better.
2. **Audit the decoder before you judge the model.** Threshold calibration and a same-turn sell clamp were the difference between $0 and beating the teacher.
3. **Lower validation loss did not reliably mean a stronger agent.** Gate on games: paired, seed-counted and in the right worlds (your real losses and the teacher's hold-outs).
4. **On one GPU, spend compute on evaluation throughput.** Batching the network across games gave an 8× faster gauntlet, which was worth more than a bigger model.
5. **Look at the losses one product at a time.** One crop explained most of the gap to the 2800 tier.
6. **Don't "fix" the teacher's mistakes at play time.** Units in our clone sometimes collide on the same task, as DSM's do. Masking those collisions cost $42k-$89k per game, because the clone was pushed into states it had never seen. If a behaviour has to change, change it in training.

Thanks for reading. Happy to answer questions in the comments.

text:
Our best single-model submission scores **0.949 public AUC**. We are sharing the accuracy recipe, our smaller 0.945 model for the efficiency track, and several changes that did not help.

The accuracy result uses one CoAtNet checkpoint trained at 384 pixels. At inference we take a native 320-pixel center crop and average probabilities from the original view and an anatomical left/right mirror. It is one learned model evaluated twice. The checkpoint itself averages three selected epochs from one training run, called SWA in our code.

## The score history

These are ordinary, full twelve-finding public leaderboard scores. Rows describe successive pipeline configurations; their differences are not all isolated causal effects.

| Configuration | Public AUC | Change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Our all-data CoAtNet, 80 slices and 78 windows | 0.939 | Starting point |
| 96 slices, native 384-pixel cache, 94 windows | 0.940 | +0.001 |
| Blend + JEV labels | 0.942 | +0.002 |
| Smaller 224-pixel crop model with epoch weight averaging | 0.940 | −0.002 |
| Add external OAI knee examples with masked labels | 0.945 | +0.005 |
| 384-pixel, full-field external-data recipe | 0.948 | +0.003 |
| Same weights, native 320-pixel inference crop | 0.948 | 0.000 |
| Same weights and crop, anatomical mirror probability averaging | **0.949** | **+0.001** |

The first density change also changed cached resolution and window count. Adding external examples increased training rows and optimizer updates, and the serving precision path changed. The 224-to-384 step also changed training crop geometry and the pretrained architecture variant. Those rows should be read as recipe comparisons rather than additive gains from individual factors.

## Training and labels

The model is a timm CoAtNet backbone with finding-specific multiple-instance attention pooling. We trained on 4,349 report-labeled competition studies; the 58 expert-labeled studies were excluded from training but reused for selection. The weak targets combine our report-derived soft labels with the public label sources credited below. In the external-data recipe, 2,399 OAI knees brought the training set to 6,748 rows. PF OA, Lateral OA and Synovitis received external supervision; unavailable finding cells were masked rather than treated as negatives. Positive class weights remained based on RSNA labels.

Both released candidates use seed 42, 16 epochs, backbone learning rate 4.01e−5, head learning rate 0.00195 and weight decay 0.0588. Training used 12 windows per study, batch size 1 and gradient accumulation over 16 studies; gold evaluation used 24 windows. The smaller model averages epochs 15, 13 and 12; the accuracy model averages epochs 14, 11 and 12. These selected averages are called SWA in our code. Adding external examples increased the scheduled optimizer updates from 4,336 to 6,736, so that comparison is not compute-matched.

## The final inference recipe

Each study has 96 preprocessed slices across five sagittal, coronal, and axial series slots. We evaluate 94 three-slice windows, process them in chunks of 16, and use finding-specific attention over the complete window bag.

For the accuracy model, native 384×384 windows are cropped to pixels `[32:352, 32:352]`. No resize is applied. Sagittal left/right mirroring reverses the three slice channels; coronal and axial mirroring flips image width. We use the center slice to determine the window plane and apply the transform before normalization. We average the two sigmoid probability vectors equally. The existing final per-finding percentile ranking preserves their ordering.

The smaller model uses a 307-pixel center crop resized to 224 pixels, the same 94-window policy, FP16 autocast, and one view. It scores 0.945. Recorded submit-to-score turnaround was about 7.2 minutes for that entry and 26.1 minutes for the mirrored accuracy entry. These include queueing and orchestration; they are **not official inference runtimes or efficiency ranks**.

## What did not help

| Tested change | Public AUC, reference → result |
|---|---:|
| Older model: 94 windows reduced to 24 | 0.940 → 0.934 |
| Older model: width-flip TTA across every imaging plane | 0.940 → 0.939 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 304 pixels | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 288 pixels | 0.948 → 0.946 |
| Epoch 14 instead of averaged weights, same 320-pixel inference | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Fresh training with corrected batch-normalization checkpoint replay | 0.948 → 0.944 |
| Fresh native 320-pixel crop training, anatomical mirror inference | 0.949 → 0.946 |

The all-plane width flip is different from anatomical mirroring, and it was tested on an older checkpoint. Its failure does not establish a controlled comparison between the mirror implementations. The new crop-trained model also failed to replace the incumbent despite encouraging gold diagnostics.

Our 58 labeled studies were reused for checkpoint selection and development. They are useful diagnostics, not independent cross-validation. For example, epoch 14 improved gold AUC while losing on the public board. Rounded public-score differences, especially +0.001, do not establish statistical significance or a private-test gain.

## Credits and release references

Thanks to [dreaddevelopment for the public Raptor CoAtNet/MIL recipe and baseline weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dreaddevelopment/raptor-knee-widedense). That public checkpoint scored 0.924 in our baseline read; it is context, rather than a controlled starting point for the table. Our selected checkpoints were retrained. The public weak-label contributions include [stevenleehans](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stevenleehans/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels), [pilkwang](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels), and [riadmohamed42's JEV labels and verification](https://www.kaggle.com/code/riadmohamed42/jev-knee-labels-verification). We thank RSNA and the competition data contributors.

Reproducibility notebooks: [accuracy, 0.949](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0949-anatomical-mirror) and [efficiency, 0.945](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0945-efficient-224crop). The [selected learned weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nartaa/rsna-knee-publication-swa-weights-20261007) are a separate minimal dependency. Both notebooks preserve the exact scored scientific inference source and checkpoint hashes, include hardware/environment requirements, and are saved statically without running inference. No OAI images, identifiers, records, raw reports, subject-level labels or predictions are distributed.

Both models used the same 2,399 baseline OAI knees; the unsuccessful 12-month arm is excluded from these release models. The public Study describes aggregate methods/results while its exact-input linkage manifest remains restricted to qualified researchers.

Data and/or research tools used in the preparation of this manuscript were obtained and analyzed from the controlled access datasets distributed from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), a data repository housed within the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). OAI is a collaborative informatics system created by the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute of Arthritis, Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) to provide a worldwide resource to quicken the pace of biomarker identification, scientific investigation and OA drug development. Dataset identifier(s): 10.15154/0hcg-f676.
